# Introduction

This project investigates the safe-haven effect of the Swiss Franc (CHF) during major geopolitical crises. We test whether global geopolitical risk shocks cause capital inflows into Switzerland independently of traditional financial dynamics such as interest rate differentials.

Our main hypothesis is that a positive shock to the GPR Index leads to statistically significant increase in portfolio investment inflows into Switzerland from foreign countries. Therefore, we should observe a "pure-fear" safe-haven effect that cannot be explained by carry trade logic alone. We control for the carry trade channel through the US-CH yield spread. The S&P 500 was considered as an additional control for financial panic but was excluded to preserve degrees of freedom given our sample size, and since the yield spread already partially reflects broader financial stress. Including the S&P 500 would reduce degrees of freedom without meaningfully improving identification, given the fact that there is an overlap between equity market stress and yield spread dynamics. 

# Data

## Variables and Sources used

We decided to use quarterly data covering the time period 1985-Q1 to 2025-Q4. The dataset contains the following variables:

- **GPR Index**: Global Geopolitical Risk Index (Caldara & Iacoviello, 2022). Measures monthly adverse geopolitical events and associated risks. It quantifies the intensity of global tensions based on newspaper coverage of war, terrorism, and international disputes.
- **Portfolio inflows Switzerland**: Net incurrence of portfolio investment liabilities (SNB Balance of Payments). This is our main dependent variable capturing safe-haven capital flows into Switzerland.
- **US-CH yield spread**: The difference between US and Swiss 10-year government bond yields. Controls for the carry trade channel — the primary alternative explanation for CHF inflows.
- **SNB FX reserves change** *(Model B only)*: Quarterly change in SNB foreign exchange reserves. Controls for mechanical flows generated by SNB interventions, particularly visible after the 2022 policy reversal.

## Sample periods

We estimate two models with different sample periods:

- **Model A (main model)**: 1985-Q1 to 2025-Q4; full sample, 3 variables (GPR, yield spread, portfolio inflows)
- **Model B (robustness)**: 1997-Q1 to 2025-Q4; includes SNB FX reserves change as 4th control variable to absorb mechanical central bank flows

The SNB FX reserves data is only available from 1996-Q4, which is why Model B starts in 1997-Q1.

# Data Loading

## Packages

We begin by installing and loading all required R packages.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

pkgs <- c("tidyverse", "readxl", "vars", "urca",
          "tseries", "ggplot2", "patchwork", "scales",
          "strucchange", "knitr", "kableExtra", "moments", "gt",
          "ggtext")

for (p in pkgs) {
  if (!p %in% rownames(installed.packages())) install.packages(p)
}

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(vars)
library(urca)
library(tseries)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
library(strucchange)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(moments)
library(gt)
library(ggtext)

# Presentation-ready theme used across all plots
theme_chf <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey40"),
    axis.title       = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    axis.text        = element_text(size = 9,  color = "grey30"),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey92", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),

    legend.position  = "bottom",
    plot.margin      = margin(10, 15, 10, 15)
  )
}
```

## GPR Index

The GPR Index is downloaded and we use the global GPR column and convert the quarter
label to a proper date format.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

gpr <- read_excel("data_gpr_quarterly.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1") %>%
  dplyr::select(quarter, GPR) %>%
  mutate(
    year  = as.integer(substr(quarter, 1, 4)),
    q     = as.integer(substr(quarter, 6, 6)),
    month = (q - 1) * 3 + 1,
    date  = as.Date(paste(year, month, "01", sep = "-"))
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(date, GPR)

head(gpr)
```

## Portfolio Inflows (dependent variable)

Net portfolio investment inflows into Switzerland from the SNB Balance of Payments.
Positive values indicate net foreign purchases of Swiss assets (safe-haven inflows).
Negative values indicate net foreign sales.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

pip <- read_excel("snb_portfolio_inflows.xlsx",
                  sheet = "R_import", skip = 4) %>%
  dplyr::select(date = 2, pip_total = 3) %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

head(pip)
```

## SNB FX Reserves

End of quarter stock level and quarterly change. Used in Model B only.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

fx_res <- read_excel("snb_fx_reserves_quarterly.xlsx",
                     sheet = "Quarterly (End of Period)", skip = 5) %>%
  dplyr::select(date = 2, fx_reserves_eop = 3, d_fx_reserves = 4) %>%
  mutate(
    date          = as.Date(date),
    d_fx_reserves = as.numeric(d_fx_reserves) / 1000  # rescaled to CHF billions
  )

head(fx_res)
```

## Yield Spread

The yield spread is the difference between the US and Swiss 10-year government bond
yields, expressed in percentage points. It controls for the carry trade channel.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

spread <- read_excel("US_CH_10Y_spread_clean.xlsx",
                     sheet = "Quarterly", skip = 5) %>%
  dplyr::select(date = 2, spread = 5) %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

head(spread)
```

## S&P 500

Loaded for variable selection testing only (Section 4). Not included in any
final VAR model specification.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

sp500 <- read_excel("S&P500_clean_quarterly.xlsx",
                    sheet = "Quarterly", skip = 4) %>%
  dplyr::select(date = 2, sp500 = 3) %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    date = as.Date(paste0(
      format(date, "%Y"), "-",
      sprintf("%02d", ((as.integer(format(date, "%m")) - 1) %/% 3) * 3 + 1),
      "-01"))
  )

head(sp500)
```

## Merge all variables

We merge all datasets by date into a single quarterly panel. All variables are aligned by the first day of each quarter.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

df <- pip %>%
  left_join(gpr,    by = "date") %>%
  left_join(spread, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(fx_res, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(sp500,  by = "date") %>%
  arrange(date)

cat("Dimensions:", nrow(df), "rows x", ncol(df), "columns\n")
cat("Date range:", as.character(min(df$date)),
    "to", as.character(max(df$date)), "\n")
cat("\nNA count per column:\n")
print(colSums(is.na(df)))
```

# Variable Transformations

Before we are able to estimate the VAR we need to transform the raw variables. Variables that are non-stationary must be converted to first differences. We also apply log transformations to compress the scale of variables with large values.

The yield spread enters the VAR in levels since it is most likely already stationary because interest rate spreads tend to mean-revert over time. We will confirm this formally in Section 7 with unit root tests.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    ln_pip     = log(abs(pip_total) + 1) * sign(pip_total),
    ln_gpr     = log(GPR),
    ln_sp500   = log(sp500),
    d_ln_pip   = c(NA, diff(ln_pip)),
    d_ln_gpr   = c(NA, diff(ln_gpr)),
    d_ln_sp500 = c(NA, diff(ln_sp500))
  )

df %>%
  dplyr::select(date, pip_total, d_ln_pip, GPR, d_ln_gpr, spread) %>%
  summary()
```
## Variable Units — Reference Summary

The table below consolidates the units of all variables in both their raw 
and transformed forms. All downstream results (VAR coefficients, IRF values, forecast errors) are expressed in these units and should be interpreted accordingly.

| Variable | Raw Unit | Transformation | VAR Unit | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Portfolio Inflows | CHF millions | log → first difference | Δ ln(pip) | Quarter-on-quarter % change in inflows |
| GPR Index | Dimensionless index | log → first difference | Δ ln(GPR) | Quarter-on-quarter % change in GPR |
| Yield Spread | Percentage points (pp) | none | levels (pp) | US 10Y minus Swiss 10Y yield in pp |
| Δ FX Reserves | CHF billions (after /1000) | none | levels (CHF bn) | Quarterly change in SNB reserves |
| Structural GPR shock SD | Dimensionless | from Cholesky | 0.2386 | ≈ 24% unexpected quarterly GPR increase |
| IRF y-axis | Δ ln(pip) units | scaled by SD | response units | Change in inflow growth per 1 SD GPR shock |
| VAR coefficients | Δ ln(pip) per unit | none | raw coefficient | Effect of 1 unit change in regressor |
| FEVD | % of variance | none | share (0–1) | Share of inflow variance explained by each shock |
| Bootstrap CI | Δ ln(pip) units | none | same as IRF | 90% confidence band around IRF point estimate |
| Companion root modulus | Dimensionless | none | 0–1 | Must be < 1 for VAR stability |
| R² | Dimensionless | none | 0–1 | Share of variance explained by model |
| Granger F-statistic | Dimensionless | none | F(8,438) | Joint test of all GPR lag coefficients = 0 |
| RMSE / MAE | Δ ln(pip) units | none | forecast error | Out-of-sample forecast accuracy |
| RMSE ratio | Dimensionless | none | 0.48 | VAR error / random walk error — < 1 means VAR wins |

**Key unit facts:**

- **Portfolio inflows** enter the VAR as Δ ln(pip) — dimensionless log differences. A value of 1.0 means approximately a 100% quarter-on-quarter increase in inflows. Values regularly swing between −20 and +20 given the extreme volatility of quarterly capital flows.

- **GPR Index** enters as Δ ln(GPR) — dimensionless. The structural shock SD of 0.2386 means a typical unexpected GPR movement is ±24% per quarter.

- **Yield Spread** enters in levels measured in percentage points. A value of 2.5 means US yields are 2.5 percentage points above Swiss yields. It does not need transformation because it is already stationary (mean-reverting).

- **FX Reserves** enter in CHF billions after dividing the raw SNB data by 1000. A value of 26.4 means a typical unexpected quarterly SNB intervention is ±26.4 CHF billion. This rescaling was applied in Section 2.4 to eliminate the units mismatch with the log-differenced variables.

- **IRF values** are in Δ ln(pip) units scaled to one structural SD GPR shock. A value of +1.553 at horizon 1 (Figure 2) therefore indicates a strong positive response in the quarterly growth rate of portfolio inflows one quarter after the shock. Under the standard log approximation, this corresponds roughly to a 155% increase in inflow growth, although the exact nonlinear interpretation is larger.

- **VAR coefficients** such as 4.808 and 8.637 are in Δ ln(pip) per unit of Δ ln(GPR). Since one unit of Δ ln(GPR) corresponds to an extremely large change in geopolitical risk relative to the observed sample, coefficients should be scaled by the structural shock standard deviation of 0.2386 for economic interpretation, yielding shock-scaled effects of 1.147 and 2.061 respectively.

# Variable Selection Justification

We formally justify the exclusion of the S&P 500 from all model specifications. Two independent arguments support this decision: a statistical argument based on non-stationarity, and a theoretical argument based on the nature of our dependent variable.

## Argument 1 — The S&P 500 is Non-Stationary

A VAR requires all included variables to be stationary. 
We test the S&P 500 index using the ADF test under both levels and first differences.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ADF helper function
run_adf_test <- function(series, variable_name, spec_type = "drift") {
  cleaned_series  <- na.omit(series)
  adf_result      <- ur.df(cleaned_series, type = spec_type, selectlags = "AIC")
  test_statistic  <- adf_result@teststat[1]
  critical_values <- adf_result@cval[1, ]

  tibble(
    Variable = variable_name,
    ADF_stat = round(test_statistic,           3),
    CV_1pct  = round(critical_values["1pct"],  3),
    CV_5pct  = round(critical_values["5pct"],  3),
    CV_10pct = round(critical_values["10pct"], 3),
    Decision = ifelse(test_statistic < critical_values["5pct"],
                      "Stationary", "Non-stationary")
  )
}

# Run ADF test on S&P 500 
adf_sp500_results <- bind_rows(
  run_adf_test(df$ln_sp500,   "ln(S&P 500) — levels"),
  run_adf_test(df$d_ln_sp500, "Δ ln(S&P 500) — 1st difference")
)

adf_sp500_results %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**ADF Unit Root Test: S&P 500**"),
    subtitle = md("*Drift specification · AIC lag selection · 5% significance threshold*")
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Variable = "Variable",
    ADF_stat = "ADF Statistic",
    CV_1pct  = "CV 1%",
    CV_5pct  = "CV 5%",
    CV_10pct = "CV 10%",
    Decision = "Decision"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "left",   columns = Variable) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(ADF_stat, CV_1pct,
                                            CV_5pct, CV_10pct, Decision)) %>%
  cols_width(
    Variable ~ px(230),
    ADF_stat ~ px(100),
    CV_1pct  ~ px(70),
    CV_5pct  ~ px(70),
    CV_10pct ~ px(70),
    Decision ~ px(120)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_fill(color = "#f5f5f5"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 1)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_fill(color = "#ffffff"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 2)
  ) %>%
  # Stationary — green with check
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#2ca02c"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = Decision,
      rows    = Decision == "Stationary"
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#d62728"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = Decision,
      rows    = Decision == "Non-stationary"
    )
  ) %>%
  text_transform(
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = Decision,
      rows    = Decision == "Stationary"
    ),
    fn = function(x) paste0("<span style='color:#2ca02c'>✓ Stationary</span>")
  ) %>%
  text_transform(
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = Decision,
      rows    = Decision == "Non-stationary"
    ),
    fn = function(x) paste0("<span style='color:#d62728'>✗ Non-stationary</span>")
  ) %>%
  # LaTeX-style borders
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "top",    color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 2)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = c("top", "bottom"),
                              color = "white", weight = px(0)),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 1)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    md("*Note: H₀: unit root present. Reject H₀ if ADF statistic < CV 5% (−2.88). ln(S&P 500) in levels is non-stationary — it follows a random walk driven by long-run growth trends. Δ ln(S&P 500) in first differences is stationary, but including it would misrepresent its economic role as a control for equity market sentiment.*")
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.font.size                 = px(13),
    table.border.top.style          = "hidden",
    table.border.bottom.style       = "hidden",
    row.striping.include_table_body = FALSE,
    column_labels.background.color  = "white",
    table_body.hlines.style         = "none",
    heading.border.bottom.style     = "none"
  )
```
The S&P 500 in levels is non-stationary since it follows a random walk driven by long-run growth trends. While applying first-differencing to the values we do achieve stationarity, but including Δ ln(S&P 500) would alter the variable's economic interpretation. We would no longer be controlling for equity market sentiment, but for short-run return shocks, which is not the theoretically relevant quantity. Including a non-stationary variable in levels risks spurious regression. And including it in first-differenced form misrepresents its role. Either way, the S&P 500 is unsuitable for our VAR.

## Argument 2 — Theoretical Irrelevance for Swiss Portfolio Inflows

Beyond the statistical argument, the S&P 500 is conceptually misaligned with our research question. Our dependent variable (portfolio investment inflows into Switzerland) captures foreign purchases of Swiss assets, motivated by the safe-haven properties of the CHF and Swiss financial markets. The S&P 500, as an stock market index tracking the performance of the 500 largest US-listed publicly traded corporations, reflects US equity market performance and domestic investor sentiment.

The safe-haven channel we study within this project operates through fear-driven capital flight into Switzerland, not through US equity dynamics. A global investor fleeing to safety responds to geopolitical risk (captured by GPR) and yield incentives (captured by the spread) and not to the level of US stock prices. Including the S&P 500 would fuse two distinct mechanisms: the safe-haven demand for CHF assets and US equity market performance, which are driven by largely independent forces.

We therefore exclude the S&P 500 from all model specifications on both statisticaland theoretical grounds.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

Before we continue with the unit root tests and VAR, this section visually inspects the time series to identify trends, volatility patterns and the major crisis episodes that are central to the safe-haven hypothesis. The shaded areas mark the key geopolitical events of our sample.

We highlight especially the 10 below listed geopolitical events:

1. Gulf War 1990
2. Kosovo War 1999
3. 9/11 2001
4. Iraq War 2003
5. GFC 2008
6. Euro Crisis 2011
7. Crimea 2014
8. COVID-19 2020
9. Ukraine-Russia 2022
10. Gaza War 2023

## Define Crisis Episodes within the Window

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

crises <- tibble(
  label = c("Gulf War", "Kosovo War", "9/11", "Iraq War", "GFC",
            "Euro Crisis", "Crimea", "COVID-19", "Ukraine", "Gaza War"),
  start = as.Date(c("1990-08-01", "1999-03-01", "2001-09-01", "2003-03-01",
                    "2008-09-01", "2011-07-01", "2014-02-01", "2020-03-01",
                    "2022-02-01", "2023-10-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("1991-02-01", "1999-06-01", "2002-01-01", "2003-12-01",
                    "2009-06-01", "2012-06-01", "2014-08-01", "2020-12-01",
                    "2022-12-01", "2025-01-01"))
)

add_crises <- function(p) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(crises))) {
    p <- p + annotate("rect",
      xmin = crises$start[i], xmax = crises$end[i],
      ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
      fill = "#d62728", alpha = 0.12)
  }
  p
}
```

## Transformed Series (VAR inputs)

This section transforms the raw data into VAR-ready series and provides a visual inspection of the transformations before conducting formal stationarity tests. A stationary series should fluctuate around a stable mean without a persistent trend; otherwise, additional differencing may be required. As discussed previously, the yield spread enters the VAR in levels, consistent with its mean-reverting behavior. In contrast, the log-differenced GPR and portfolio inflow series both oscillate around zero with no visible trend, providing preliminary evidence of stationarity. This visual analysis motivates the formal unit root tests presented in Section 7, which confirm the appropriate transformation for each variable.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8

df %>%
  dplyr::select(date, d_ln_pip, d_ln_gpr, spread) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "var", values_to = "val") %>%
  mutate(var = recode(var,
    d_ln_pip = "Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows)",
    d_ln_gpr = "Δ ln(GPR)",
    spread   = "Yield Spread (levels)"
  )) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = val)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~var, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title    = "Transformed Variables — VAR Inputs (Model A)",
       subtitle = "Series used in estimation · all stationary",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_chf()
```

# Unit Root Tests

We formally assess the stationarity properties of the time series using the Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) unit root test. The ADF test evaluates whether a series follows a random walk process (non-stationary), where shocks have permanent effects, or whether it reverts toward a stable mean over time (stationary). The null hypothesis corresponds to the presence of a unit root, implying non-stationarity.

The ADF specification includes lagged differences of the dependent variable to account for serial correlation in the residuals. Including an appropriate number of lags is important because too few lags may leave residual autocorrelation, while too many lags may reduce estimation efficiency. The formal lag-selection procedure used in the VAR model is discussed separately in the following section. 

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ADF test results for all VAR variables 
# Tests both levels and first differences to confirm correct transformation
# use run_adf_test function defined in Section 5.1

adf_all_variables <- bind_rows(
  run_adf_test(df$ln_pip,        "ln(Portfolio Inflows) — levels"),
  run_adf_test(df$ln_gpr,        "ln(GPR) — levels"),
  run_adf_test(df$spread,        "Yield Spread — levels"),
  run_adf_test(df$d_fx_reserves, "Δ FX Reserves — levels"),
  run_adf_test(df$d_ln_pip,      "Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows) — 1st difference"),
  run_adf_test(df$d_ln_gpr,      "Δ ln(GPR) — 1st difference")
) %>%
  mutate(
    Decision = ifelse(Decision == "Stationary",
                      "Stationary", "Non-stationary")
  )

adf_all_variables %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 2 — ADF Unit Root Tests**"),
    subtitle = md("*Drift specification · AIC lag selection · 5% significance threshold*")

  ) %>%

                                            CV_5pct, CV_10pct, Decision)) %>%

) %>%

) %>%

  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.font.size                 = px(13),
    table.border.top.style          = "hidden",
    table.border.bottom.style       = "hidden",
    row.striping.include_table_body = FALSE,
    column_labels.background.color  = "white",
    table_body.hlines.style         = "none",

```
Although the ADF test does not find evidence of a unit root for ln(Portfolio Inflows) and ln(GPR) in levels, both variables are still transformed into first differences for two main reasons. First, both series show noticeable upward trends over the 1985–2025 sample, as seen in the time-series plots in Section 6. Portfolio inflows increase from CHF 2,324 million in 1985-Q1 to a peak of CHF 48,849 million, with some very large negative outflows reaching −CHF 45,418 million. Similarly, the GPR index ranges from 46.3 to 351.8 and stays elevated during major geopolitical crises. In addition, Schwert (1989) argues that ADF-type unit root tests can have low power in small samples and may struggle with highly persistent series, making stationarity conclusions less reliable. Second, using log-differences gives the variables a clear economic interpretation as quarterly percentage changes, which is common in the macro-financial VAR literature on safe-haven flows. The yield spread enters in levels because interest-rate differentials are naturally mean-reverting, while ΔFX Reserves is already measured as a quarterly change and therefore enters the VAR directly in levels.

Schwert, G.W. (1989). Tests for unit roots: A Monte Carlo investigation. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics*, 7(2), 147–159. 
<https://www.jstor.org/stable/1391432>

# VAR Lag Length Selection

We use the VARselect() function to determine the optimal lag length for the VAR models based on several standard information criteria: Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Hannan–Quinn Criterion (HQ), Schwarz Criterion (SC/BIC), and the Final Prediction Error (FPE). The procedure evaluates lag lengths from 1 to 8 and computes each criterion for every specification.

The different criteria balance model fit and model complexity in different ways. The AIC is generally more permissive and tends to select longer lag structures, while the SC/BIC applies a stronger penalty for additional parameters and therefore favors more parsimonious models. The HQ criterion lies between these two approaches. The FPE criterion is closely related to the AIC and focuses on out-of-sample forecasting performance.

Lag selection is performed separately for Model A and Model B.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Model A: GPR → Spread → PIP (3 variables, 1985–2025)
# Cholesky identification ordering:
#   1. d_ln_gpr : global geopolitical index (most exogenous)
#   2. spread.  : slow-moving carry trade variable
#   3. d_ln_pip : endogenous safe-haven response 

data_A <- df %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("1985-01-01"),
         date <= as.Date("2025-10-01")) %>%
  dplyr::select(d_ln_gpr, spread, d_ln_pip) %>%
  na.omit()

cat("=== Model A — lag selection (3 variables) ===\n")
lag_A <- VARselect(data_A, lag.max = 8, type = "const")
print(lag_A$selection)

# Model B: GPR → Spread → ΔFX → PIP (4 variables, 1997–2025) 

data_B <- df %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("1997-01-01"),
         date <= as.Date("2025-10-01")) %>%
  dplyr::select(d_ln_gpr, spread, d_fx_reserves, d_ln_pip) %>%
  na.omit()

cat("\n=== Model B — lag selection (4 variables) ===\n")
lag_B <- VARselect(data_B, lag.max = 8, type = "const")
print(lag_B$selection)

p_A <- min(lag_A$selection["AIC(n)"], 4)
p_B <- min(lag_B$selection["AIC(n)"], 4)
cat("\nFinal lags — Model A:", p_A, "| Model B:", p_B, "\n")
```
The lag selection criteria point toward a relatively persistent dynamic structure. Both the AIC and FPE consistently select 5 lags for both models, which we cap at 4 (one full year) in order to preserve degrees of freedom given our sample of 164 quarterly observations. The stricter SC criterion instead prefers a single lag, reflecting its heavier penalty for model complexity. This disagreement across criteria is common in VAR applications with macroeconomic data and does not necessarily indicate a specification issue, but rather the usual trade-off between model fit and parsimony.

We adopt the AIC-based selection (capped at p = 4) as our baseline specification, since safe-haven capital flows are likely to adjust gradually and a one-year dynamic window is economically plausible in our setting. The SC-based lag specification is used as a robustness check in Section 11 to verify that the main results are not sensitive to lag length choice.

# VAR Estimation

## Model Specification

Following Definition 3.1 of the lecture notes, we estimate a VAR($p$) model where $y_t$ denotes an $n \times 1$ vector of endogenous variables. For Model A with $n = 3$ variables and $p = 4$ lags, the system is shown as follow:

$$
y_t = c + \Phi_1 y_{t-1} + \Phi_2 y_{t-2} + \Phi_3 y_{t-3} + \Phi_4 y_{t-4} + \varepsilon_t
\tag{1}
$$

where:

$$
y_t = \begin{pmatrix} \Delta \ln(\text{GPR}_t) \\ \text{Spread}_t \\ \Delta \ln(\text{PIP}_t) \end{pmatrix}, \quad
c = \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\varepsilon_t = \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_{1,t} \\ \varepsilon_{2,t} \\ \varepsilon_{3,t} \end{pmatrix}
$$

$c$ is a $(3 \times 1)$ vector of constants, $\Phi_1, \ldots, \Phi_4$ are 
$(3 \times 3)$ coefficient matrices, and $\varepsilon_t$ is a $(3 \times 1)$ vector of reduced-form residuals with $\varepsilon_t \sim (0, \Sigma)$, where $\Sigma$ is the $(3 \times 3)$ residual covariance matrix. Note that the components of $\varepsilon_t$ are serially uncorrelated but may be contemporaneously correlated across equations, which is the identification problem addressed in Section 8.4.

### The Key Equation — Portfolio Inflows

Writing out the third row of Eq. (1) explicitly gives the equation 
that is central to our hypothesis:

$$
\Delta \ln(\text{PIP}_t) = c_3 
+ \sum_{j=1}^{4} \alpha_j \, \Delta \ln(\text{GPR}_{t-j}) 
+ \sum_{j=1}^{4} \beta_j \, \text{Spread}_{t-j} 
+ \sum_{j=1}^{4} \gamma_j \, \Delta \ln(\text{PIP}_{t-j}) 
+ \varepsilon_{3,t}
\tag{2}
$$

where $\alpha_j$ are the GPR coefficients capturing the safe-haven fear 
channel, $\beta_j$ are the yield spread coefficients capturing the carry 
trade channel, and lastly $\gamma_j$ capture the own persistence of portfolio inflows. Our main null hypothesis is:

$$
H_0: \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \alpha_3 = \alpha_4 = 0 \quad \text{(no safe-haven effect)}
$$
$$
H_1: \alpha_j > 0 \text{ for at least one } j \quad \text{(safe-haven effect present)}
$$

$H_0$ is tested jointly via the Granger causality F-test in Section 14, and individually via the coefficient significance tests in Section 9.2.

### Structural Shocks

Following the lecture notation, the reduced-form residuals $\varepsilon_t$ are related to the structural shocks $\eta_t$ via:

$$\varepsilon_t = B\eta_t$$
where $B$ is the impulse matrix and $\eta_t \sim (0, Id)$ are mutually 
and serially independent structural shocks. As noted in the lecture, 
while $\varepsilon_t$ and $\eta_t$ are serially uncorrelated, in both 
cases the vectors $\eta_t$ and $\varepsilon_t$ are serially correlated 
through time. We recover $B$ via the Cholesky decomposition of $\Sigma$ 
in Section 9.5, which sets $B = P$ where $\Sigma = PP'$.

### Model B Extension

Model B extends Eq. (1) to $n = 4$ variables by inserting 
$\Delta \text{FX}_t$ — the quarterly change in SNB foreign exchange 
reserves — between the yield spread and portfolio inflows:

$$
y_t = \begin{pmatrix} \Delta \ln(\text{GPR}_t) \\ \text{Spread}_t \\ \Delta \text{FX}_t \\ \Delta \ln(\text{PIP}_t) \end{pmatrix}
$$

The $\Phi_j$ matrices are now $(4 \times 4)$ and the system is estimated 
over a shorter sample 1997–2025 due to FX reserves data availability. 
Adding $\Delta \text{FX}_t$ absorbs mechanical capital flows generated by 
SNB interventions, providing a robustness check on whether the GPR 
coefficients $\alpha_j$ survive after controlling for central bank behavior and taken actions through out time.

### Stability Condition

Following Eq. (3.8) of the lecture notes, the VAR is stable if and only if the eigenvalues of the companion matrix:

$$
\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} \Phi_1 & \Phi_2 & \cdots & \Phi_p \\ I & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \ddots & & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & I & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$
lie strictly inside the unit circle. This condition is verified graphically in Section 9.4 for both models.

### Lag Length Selection

Following Eq. (3.16) of the lecture notes, we select the lag length $p$ using the Akaike Information Criterion:

$$AIC = cst + \log|\hat{\Omega}| + \frac{2}{T}N$$

where $N = p \times n^2$ is the total number of estimated parameters. AIC selects $p = 5$ for both models, capped at $p = 4$ to preserve degrees of freedom given our sample size of $T = 164$ quarters. The lag selection procedure is documented in Section 8.

## Model A — Main Model (1985–2025, 3 variables)

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

var_A <- VAR(data_A, p = p_A, type = "const")
summary(var_A)

roots_A <- roots(var_A)
cat("\nMax companion root:", round(max(roots_A), 4),
    "— Stable:", ifelse(max(roots_A) < 1, "YES ✓", "NO ✗"), "\n")
```

Compute the table format for each variable: 

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

var_A <- VAR(data_A, p = p_A, type = "const")

tidy_var_equation <- function(var_model, eq_name) {
  coef_mat  <- coef(var_model)[[eq_name]]
  raw_terms <- rownames(coef_mat)

  tibble(
    raw          = raw_terms,
    Estimate     = paste0(
                     round(coef_mat[, "Estimate"], 3),
                     as.character(symnum(coef_mat[, "Pr(>|t|)"],
                       cutpoints = c(0, .001, .01, .05, .1, 1),
                       symbols   = c("***", "**", "*", ".", "")))
                   ),
    `Std. Error` = round(coef_mat[, "Std. Error"], 3),
    `t value`    = round(coef_mat[, "t value"],    3),
    `p value`    = round(coef_mat[, "Pr(>|t|)"],   4)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    lag_group = case_when(
      grepl("\\.l(\\d+)$", raw) ~ paste0("Lag ", gsub(".*\\.l(\\d+)$", "\\1", raw)),
      raw == "const"            ~ "Constant",
      TRUE                      ~ "Other"
    ),
    Term = raw %>%
      gsub("\\.l\\d+$",     "",              .) %>%
      gsub("d_ln_gpr",      "Δ ln(GPR)",    .) %>%
      gsub("d_ln_pip",      "Δ ln(Inflows)"  ,.) %>%
      gsub("spread",        "Yield Spread",  .) %>%
      gsub("d_fx_reserves", "Δ FX Reserves", .) %>%
      gsub("const",         "Constant",      .)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(lag_group, Term, Estimate, `Std. Error`, `t value`, `p value`)
}

By contrast, neither the yield spread nor portfolio inflows exhibit statistically significant effects in the GPR equation, supporting the treatment of GPR as the most exogenous variable in the VAR ordering.",
  spread   = "The yield spread is highly persistent and is mainly explained by its own past values. The lag-1 coefficient is strongly significant at 1.157\\*\\*\\*, while the significant coefficients at lags 2 and 4 suggest that the spread adjusts gradually over time. In contrast, neither GPR nor portfolio inflows are statistically significant at any lag. This indicates that interest rate differentials evolve largely independently from geopolitical shocks and safe-haven capital flows, supporting the use of the yield spread as a control variable in the VAR model.",
  d_ln_pip = "This is the central equation of the VAR model. GPR shocks at lag 1 (4.808) and lag 4 (8.637) significantly increase Swiss portfolio inflows, providing direct evidence of a safe-haven effect. The positive lag-4 coefficient suggests that part of the adjustment unfolds gradually over time rather than occurring entirely within one quarter. By contrast, the yield spread is not statistically significant at any lag. Portfolio inflows also display strong own dynamics, with highly significant negative coefficients at lags 1–3 and a marginally positive effect at lag 4 (0.156.). Overall, the model explains approximately 52% of the variation in inflows (R² = 0.517)."
)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
```

```{r}
var_B <- VAR(data_B, p = p_B, type = "const")

tidy_var_equation_B <- function(var_model, eq_name) {
  coef_mat  <- coef(var_model)[[eq_name]]
  raw_terms <- rownames(coef_mat)
  pvals     <- coef_mat[, "Pr(>|t|)"]
  stars     <- as.character(symnum(pvals,
                  cutpoints = c(0, .001, .01, .05, .1, 1),
                  symbols   = c("***", "**", "*", ".", "")))

  tibble(
    raw          = raw_terms,
    Term         = raw_terms %>%
                     gsub("\\.l\\d+$",     "",              .) %>%
                     gsub("d_ln_gpr",      "Δ ln(GPR)",    .) %>%
                     gsub("d_ln_pip",      "Δ ln(Inflows)", .) %>%
                     gsub("spread",        "Yield Spread",  .) %>%
                     gsub("d_fx_reserves", "Δ FX Reserves", .) %>%
                     gsub("const",         "Constant",      .),
    Estimate     = paste0(round(coef_mat[, "Estimate"], 3), stars),
    `Std. Error` = round(coef_mat[, "Std. Error"], 3),
    `t value`    = round(coef_mat[, "t value"],    3),
    `p value`    = round(pvals, 4),
    lag_group    = case_when(
      grepl("\\.l(\\d+)$", raw_terms) ~
        paste0("Lag ", gsub(".*\\.l(\\d+)$", "\\1", raw_terms)),
      raw_terms == "const" ~ "Constant",
      TRUE                 ~ "Other"
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(lag_group, Term, Estimate,
                `Std. Error`, `t value`, `p value`)
}
```

```{r}
get_coef <- function(var_model, eq, term) {
  coef_mat <- coef(var_model)[[eq]]
  est      <- round(coef_mat[term, "Estimate"], 3)

  paste0(est, stars)
}
```

## VAR Stability - Companion Roots 

All eigenvalues of the companion matrix must lie strictly inside the unit circle for the VAR to be stable and the impulse responses to be meaningful. The plot below confirms this condition holds for both models A and B.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

# Extract companion matrix roots for both models
roots_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    model  = "Model A (1985–2025)",
    root   = roots(var_A, modulus = FALSE)
  ),
  tibble(
    model  = "Model B (1997–2025)",
    root   = roots(var_B, modulus = FALSE)
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    real    = Re(root),
    imag    = Im(root),
    modulus = Mod(root)
  )

# Unit circle points
unit_circle <- tibble(
  angle = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 300),
  x     = cos(angle),
  y     = sin(angle)
)

ggplot() +
  # Unit circle
  geom_path(data = unit_circle,
            aes(x = x, y = y),
            color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed") +
  # Axes
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  # Roots
  geom_point(data = roots_df,
             aes(x = real, y = imag, color = model),
             size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Model A (1985–2025)" = "#1f77b4",
               "Model B (1997–2025)" = "#d62728"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.2, 1.2), ylim = c(-1.2, 1.2)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure 1 — Inverse Roots of VAR Companion Matrix",
    subtitle = "All roots must lie strictly inside the unit circle for VAR stability",
    caption = paste0("Model A: max modulus = ", round(max(roots(var_A)), 3),
                 " · Model B: max modulus = ", round(max(roots(var_B)), 3),
                 " · Both models are stable."),
    x        = "Real part",
    y        = "Imaginary part"
  ) +
  theme_chf() +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.82, 0.12),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "grey85",
                                     linewidth = 0.3),
    legend.margin   = margin(4, 8, 4, 8),
    plot.caption    = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40",
                                   hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 8))
  )
```
Figure 1 plots plots the eigenvalues of the VAR companion matrix in the complex plane to verify model stability. Although VAR coefficients 
are real-valued, eigenvalues are generally complex numbers $a + bi$, with real and imaginary components on the respective axes. Stability requires that the modulus of each eigenvalue $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, therefore its 
distance from the origin, is strictly less than one. All eigenvalues lying inside the unit circle confirms this condition is satisfied, guaranteeing that impulse responses decay toward zero and validating the VAR specification. Meaning essentially that the system returns to equilibrium after a shock rather than diverging. 

## Identification — Cholesky Decomposition

To give the VAR residuals a causal interpretation, we need to transform them from correlated reduced-form residuals retrieved from the VAR estimations into uncorrelated structural shocks. This is done through a Cholesky decomposition of the residual covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}'$, where $\mathbf{P}$ is a lower triangular matrix. The lower triangular matrix P below makes this identification assumption explicit.The zero restrictions in the upper triangle of $\mathbf{P}$ encode the identification assumption: variables ordered earlier in the system can affect all subsequent variables within the same quarter, but cannot themselves be affected by variables ordered later. We impose the following ordering for model A:

$$\Delta \ln(\text{GPR}) \rightarrow \text{Yield Spread} \rightarrow \Delta \ln(\text{Portfolio Inflows})$$
And for model B we impose: 
$$\Delta \ln(\text{GPR}) \rightarrow \text{Yield Spread} \rightarrow \Delta \text{FX Reserves} \rightarrow \Delta \ln(\text{Portfolio Inflows})$$
Those orderings reflect the economic logic of the safe-haven channel. Geopolitical risk is driven by global political events that are independent of Swiss financial market conditions. GPR can therefore affect both the yield spread and portfolio inflows contemporaneously but is not itself affected by either within the same quarter. The yield spread reflects monetary policy dynamics that respond to geopolitical conditions but move independently of short-run capital flows. Portfolio inflows are the most endogenous variable within the model and they absorb the effects of both GPR and yield spread (Model A) and additionally the FX reserves (Model B) shocks within the quarter, but do not feed back into either until the following quarter. The diagonal elements within the tables confirm the structural shock standard deviations used to scale the IRFs in Section 10.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Model A Cholesky Decomposition
# Residual covariance matrix from VAR estimation
residual_cov_A <- summary(var_A)$covres

# Lower triangular Cholesky factor P such that Sigma = P * P'
# Diagonal of P = structural shock standard deviations
# Off-diagonal lower elements = permitted contemporaneous transmission
cholesky_lower_A <- t(chol(residual_cov_A))

# Model B Cholesky Decomposition
residual_cov_B <- summary(var_B)$covres
cholesky_lower_B <- t(chol(residual_cov_B))

# Model A: 
tibble(
  Variable = c("Δ ln(GPR)", "Yield Spread", "Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows)"),
  GPR      = round(cholesky_lower_A[, 1], 4),
  Spread   = round(cholesky_lower_A[, 2], 4),
  Inflows  = round(cholesky_lower_A[, 3], 4)
) %>%
  gt() %>%

    style     = cell_borders(sides = "top", color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "top",    color = "black", weight = px(1.5)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "black", weight = px(1.5)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 4)

  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    md("*Diagonal elements (bold writing) = structural shock standard deviations. Four-variable recursive ordering: GPR → Yield Spread → Δ FX Reserves → Portfolio Inflows. After rescaling FX reserves to CHF billions in Section 3.4, the entries are now in a comparable order of magnitude to the other variables. This does not affect IRF identification for portfolio inflows.*")
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.font.size                 = px(13),
    table.border.top.style          = "hidden",
    table.border.bottom.style       = "hidden",
    row.striping.include_table_body = FALSE,

    table_body.hlines.style         = "none",
```

## IRF Decomposition - Connecting VAR Coefficients to Impulse Responses

Section 9.6 creates the formal link between the VAR coefficient tables of Sections 9.2 and 9.3 and the impulse response functions presented in Section 10. The VAR estimation produces the reduced-form of the coefficients — the $\alpha_j$, $\beta_j$ and $\gamma_j$ values visible in the coefficient tables — but these alone are insufficient to determine the dynamic response of the system to a structural shock. As established in Section 8.4, structural identification additionally requires the cholesky decomposition of the residual covariance matrix, which imposes a recursive ordering on the system that can be thought of as a chain reaction structure. As noted by Mohr (2020), the variable ordered first — $\Delta \ln(\text{GPR})$ — is by construction not sensitive to a contemporaneous shock from any other variable, while portfolio inflows ordered last in the Cholesky decomposition absorb the contemporaneous effects of all preceding variables within the same quarter. Each off-diagonal element of the Cholesky matrix $\mathbf{P}$ determines how much of the shock passes through to the next variable in the chain, and the zeros in the upper triangle ensure the chain runs in one direction only, meaning from the most exogenous variable to the most endogenous. This ordering assumption directly shapes the IRF through $\mathbf{P}$, which scales and transmits the structural GPR shock through the system via the MA recursion of Proposition 3.1. 

To make this transmission fully explicit and verify its internal consistency, we decompose the total IRF at each horizon into its direct GPR contribution $\alpha_j \times \text{SD}_\text{GPR}$ and its indirect contribution through the yield spread and own-lag channels, which is the residual between the total IRF and the direct term that requires the computation of the full MA recursion. Mohr (2020) notes that orthogonalised impulse responses may be sensitive to the ordering of variables and recommends estimating the VAR under different orderings to assess robustness. This concern is directly addressed in Section 10 through the Model B specification, which confirms the two-wave safe-haven pattern persists under a four-variable ordering with FX reserves inserted before portfolio inflows.

*(Mohr, F.X. (2020). An Introduction to Impulse Response Analysis of VAR 
Models. r-econometrics.com. 
https://www.r-econometrics.com/timeseries/irf/)*

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Step 1: Extract VAR coefficient matrices from Model A 
# Each Phi matrix is 3x3 (one row per equation, one column per variable)
# Columns ordered as: d_ln_gpr, spread, d_ln_pip at each lag

model_a_lag1_coefs <- Bcoef(var_A)[, 1:3]   # Φ₁
model_a_lag2_coefs <- Bcoef(var_A)[, 4:6]   # Φ₂
model_a_lag3_coefs <- Bcoef(var_A)[, 7:9]   # Φ₃
model_a_lag4_coefs <- Bcoef(var_A)[, 10:12] # Φ₄

# Step 2: Cholesky matrix for Model A 
# Lower triangular P such that Sigma = P * P'
# First column P[:,1] is the GPR structural shock vector
model_a_cholesky <- t(chol(summary(var_A)$covres))

# Step 3: MA recursion for Model A (Proposition 3.1 lecture notes) 
# Ψ₀ = Identity matrix (no dynamics at horizon 0)
# Ψₕ = Φ₁Ψₕ₋₁ + Φ₂Ψₕ₋₂ + Φ₃Ψₕ₋₃ + Φ₄Ψₕ₋₄

ma_matrix_h0_A <- diag(3)
ma_matrix_h1_A <- model_a_lag1_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h0_A
ma_matrix_h2_A <- model_a_lag1_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h1_A +
                  model_a_lag2_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h0_A
ma_matrix_h3_A <- model_a_lag1_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h2_A +
                  model_a_lag2_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h1_A +
                  model_a_lag3_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h0_A
ma_matrix_h4_A <- model_a_lag1_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h3_A +
                  model_a_lag2_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h2_A +
                  model_a_lag3_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h1_A +
                  model_a_lag4_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h0_A

# Step 4: Compute IRF values for Model A 
# IRF(h) = Ψₕ · P[:,1]
# Row 3 = portfolio inflows equation
# Column 1 = GPR structural shock

# Direct GPR contribution only: α_j × SD_GPR (first term of the full product)
gpr_shock_sd_A      <- model_a_cholesky[1,1]   # = 0.2386

direct_contrib_A <- c(
  0,                                                          # horizon 0: no lag-0 coefficient
  round(model_a_lag1_coefs[3,1] * gpr_shock_sd_A, 4),       # α₁ × SD
  round(model_a_lag2_coefs[3,1] * gpr_shock_sd_A, 4),       # α₂ × SD
  round(model_a_lag3_coefs[3,1] * gpr_shock_sd_A, 4),       # α₃ × SD
  round(model_a_lag4_coefs[3,1] * gpr_shock_sd_A, 4)        # α₄ × SD
)

# Total IRF: full MA recursion including all indirect transmission paths
total_irf_A <- c(
  round((ma_matrix_h0_A %*% model_a_cholesky)[3,1], 4),
  round((ma_matrix_h1_A %*% model_a_cholesky)[3,1], 4),
  round((ma_matrix_h2_A %*% model_a_cholesky)[3,1], 4),
  round((ma_matrix_h3_A %*% model_a_cholesky)[3,1], 4),
  round((ma_matrix_h4_A %*% model_a_cholesky)[3,1], 4)
)

# Indirect contribution: total minus direct
indirect_contrib_A <- round(total_irf_A - direct_contrib_A, 4)

# Step 5: Extract VAR coefficient matrices from Model B 
# Model B has 4 variables so each Phi matrix is 4x4
# Variable ordering: d_ln_gpr, spread, d_fx_reserves, d_ln_pip

model_b_lag1_coefs <- Bcoef(var_B)[, 1:4]
model_b_lag2_coefs <- Bcoef(var_B)[, 5:8]
model_b_lag3_coefs <- Bcoef(var_B)[, 9:12]
model_b_lag4_coefs <- Bcoef(var_B)[, 13:16]

# Step 6: Cholesky matrix for Model B 

model_b_cholesky <- t(chol(summary(var_B)$covres))

# Step 7: MA recursion for Model B 

ma_matrix_h0_B <- diag(4)
ma_matrix_h1_B <- model_b_lag1_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h0_B
ma_matrix_h2_B <- model_b_lag1_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h1_B +
                  model_b_lag2_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h0_B
ma_matrix_h3_B <- model_b_lag1_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h2_B +
                  model_b_lag2_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h1_B +
                  model_b_lag3_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h0_B
ma_matrix_h4_B <- model_b_lag1_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h3_B +
                  model_b_lag2_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h2_B +
                  model_b_lag3_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h1_B +
                  model_b_lag4_coefs %*% ma_matrix_h0_B

# Step 8: Compute IRF values for Model B 
# Row 4 = portfolio inflows (4th variable in Model B)
# Column 1 = GPR structural shock

gpr_shock_sd_B <- model_b_cholesky[1,1]   # = 0.2444

direct_contrib_B <- c(
  0,
  round(model_b_lag1_coefs[4,1] * gpr_shock_sd_B, 4),
  round(model_b_lag2_coefs[4,1] * gpr_shock_sd_B, 4),
  round(model_b_lag3_coefs[4,1] * gpr_shock_sd_B, 4),
  round(model_b_lag4_coefs[4,1] * gpr_shock_sd_B, 4)
)

total_irf_B <- c(
  round((ma_matrix_h0_B %*% model_b_cholesky)[4,1], 4),
  round((ma_matrix_h1_B %*% model_b_cholesky)[4,1], 4),
  round((ma_matrix_h2_B %*% model_b_cholesky)[4,1], 4),
  round((ma_matrix_h3_B %*% model_b_cholesky)[4,1], 4),
  round((ma_matrix_h4_B %*% model_b_cholesky)[4,1], 4)
)

indirect_contrib_B <- round(total_irf_B - direct_contrib_B, 4)

# Step 9: Build display tibble 

irf_decomposition_tbl <- tibble(
  Horizon        = c("0 — Contemporaneous",
                     "1 — First wave",
                     "2 — Reversal",
                     "3 — Second wave",
                     "4 — Decay"),
  `Direct (A)`   = direct_contrib_A,
  `Indirect (A)` = indirect_contrib_A,
  `Total (A)`    = total_irf_A,
  `Direct (B)`   = direct_contrib_B,
  `Indirect (B)` = indirect_contrib_B,
  `Total (B)`    = total_irf_B
)

# Step 10: Render gt table 

irf_decomposition_tbl %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 4 — IRF Decomposition: Direct vs Indirect GPR Contribution**"),
    subtitle = md("*Response of Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows) to a one SD GPR shock · horizons 0–4 · MA recursion*")
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "Model A · 1985–2025 · 3 variables",
    columns = c(`Direct (A)`, `Indirect (A)`, `Total (A)`)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "Model B · 1997–2025 · 4 variables",
    columns = c(`Direct (B)`, `Indirect (B)`, `Total (B)`)
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Horizon        = "Horizon",
    `Direct (A)`   = "Direct",
    `Indirect (A)` = "Indirect",
    `Total (A)`    = "Total IRF",
    `Direct (B)`   = "Direct",
    `Indirect (B)` = "Indirect",
    `Total (B)`    = "Total IRF"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "left",   columns = Horizon) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center",
             columns = c(`Direct (A)`, `Indirect (A)`, `Total (A)`,
                         `Direct (B)`, `Indirect (B)`, `Total (B)`)) %>%
  cols_width(
    Horizon        ~ px(180),
    `Direct (A)`   ~ px(75),
    `Indirect (A)` ~ px(75),
    `Total (A)`    ~ px(80),
    `Direct (B)`   ~ px(75),
    `Indirect (B)` ~ px(75),
    `Total (B)`    ~ px(80)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_fill(color = "#f0f6fb"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = c(2, 4))
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_fill(color = "#fdf4f4"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 3)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#1f77b4"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = `Total (A)`, rows = `Total (A)` > 0)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#d62728"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = `Total (A)`, rows = `Total (A)` < 0)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#1f77b4"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = `Total (B)`, rows = `Total (B)` > 0)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#d62728"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = `Total (B)`, rows = `Total (B)` < 0)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_fill(color = "#f5f5f5"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "top",    color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "top",    color = "black", weight = px(1.5)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "black", weight = px(1.5)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 5)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = c("top", "bottom"),
                              color = "white", weight = px(0)),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 1:4)
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    md("*Note: The table decomposes the impulse response of Swiss portfolio inflows into a direct geopolitical risk effect and an indirect propagation effect operating through the VAR system. The indirect component captures transmission through the yield spread and autoregressive channels. The total impulse response equals the sum of both effects. Blue values indicate positive inflow responses, while red values indicate negative responses. The decomposition highlights the two-wave safe-haven pattern, with positive peaks at horizons 1 and 3 separated by a reversal at horizon 2.*")
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.font.size                 = px(13),
    table.border.top.style          = "hidden",
    table.border.bottom.style       = "hidden",
    row.striping.include_table_body = FALSE,
    column_labels.background.color  = "white",
    table_body.hlines.style         = "none",
    heading.border.bottom.style     = "none"
  )
```
**From Estimation to Impulse Responses — Closing the Loop**

Table 4 makes explicit how the VAR coefficients produce the impulse responses of Section 9. The connection runs through two steps.

First, the Cholesky decomposition in Section 9.5 produces the impulse matrix $B$ — as established in Proposition 3.1 of the lecture notes, $B = \Psi_0$ captures the contemporaneous impact of each structural shock on the system within the same quarter. The first column of $B$ is the GPR shock vector $(0.2386, \ 0.0073, \ -0.7941)'$, which scales and transmits the GPR shock to all three variables simultaneously.

Second, the MA recursion of Proposition 3.1 propagates this shock forward through the system quarter by quarter via $\Psi_h = \Phi_1\Psi_{h-1} + \cdots + \Phi_4\Psi_{h-4}$. The total IRF at each horizon is the product of $\Psi_h$ and the GPR shock vector, therefore decomposing into a direct GPR contribution $\alpha_j \times 0.2386$ and an indirect contribution through the own-lag and yield spread channels.

Two findings stand out. The direct contribution understates the true IRF at every horizon — at horizon 1, $4.808 \times 0.2386 = 1.147$ versus the true IRF of $+1.553$, with the gap reflecting own-lag feedback. And the peak occurs at horizon 3 rather than horizon 4 despite the lag-4 coefficient being the largest in the VAR, because the indirect channel generates an opposing force of $-1.480$ that nearly cancels the direct contribution of $+2.061$ at horizon 4.

Both models produce the identical two-wave structure, confirming that the safe-haven pattern is a fully traceable consequence of the VAR coefficients, the impulse matrix $B$, and Proposition 3.1.

# Impulse Response Analysis

## IRF portfolio inflows Model A

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

set.seed(42)
irf_A <- irf(var_A,
             impulse  = "d_ln_gpr",
             response = "d_ln_pip",
             n.ahead  = 12,
             ortho     = TRUE,
             boot     = TRUE,
             ci       = 0.90,
             runs     = 100)

irf_A_df <- tibble(
  horizon = 0:12,
  irf     = as.numeric(irf_A$irf$d_ln_gpr),
  lower   = as.numeric(irf_A$Lower$d_ln_gpr),
  upper   = as.numeric(irf_A$Upper$d_ln_gpr)
)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(irf_A_df, aes(x = horizon)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              fill = "#1f77b4", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(aes(y = irf),
            color = "#1f77b4", linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(y = irf),
             color = "#1f77b4", size = 2.0, shape = 21,
             fill = "white", stroke = 1.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:12) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 6)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure 2 — Impulse Response: Portfolio Inflows to a GPR Shock",
    subtitle = "Model A (1985–2025) · One standard deviation GPR shock · 90% bootstrap confidence band (100 runs)",
    x        = "Quarters after shock",
    y        = "Response of Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows)"
  ) +
  theme_chf()
```
*Figure 2: A one standard deviation GPR shock (SD = 0.2386) produces a two-wave response in Swiss portfolio inflows, with a first peak of +1.553 log-points at horizon 1 and a second peak of +1.459 log-points at horizon 3, separated by a temporary reversal of −1.484 log-points at horizon 2, before gradually decaying toward zero by horizon 12, confirming VAR stability. Responses are measured in units of Δln(Portfolio Inflows), approximating percentage changes in quarterly inflow growth. A possible economic interpretation of this pattern is that it reflects heterogeneous investor dynamics: an immediate panic-driven safe-haven response, followed by a short-term correction, and then a delayed institutional reallocation as capital adjusts more gradually over time. However, this remains a proposed interpretation rather than a definitive causal explanation. Wide 90% bootstrap confidence bands reflect the inherent volatility of quarterly capital flow data.*

Three papers provide possible explanations in regard of the pattern of the IRF, more specifically why the IRF pattern contains positive and negative peaks with similar magnitudes before gradually decaying over time: 

1. Presidential Address: Asset price dynamics with slow-moving capital (August 2010), Darrell Duffie

2. Market Liquidity and Funding Liquidity (February 2007), Markus K. Brunnermeier & Lasse Heje Pedersen 

3. Safe haven currencies (September 2009), Angelo Ranaldo & Paul Söderlind

The impulse response function suggests that the effect of geopolitical risk on Swiss portfolio inflows unfolds dynamically rather than instantaneously. The initial positive response is broadly consistent with the safe-haven role of Swiss assets, as documented by Ranaldo and Söderlind (2010), who show that the Swiss franc systematically appreciates during periods of heightened market stress, rising FX volatility, and geopolitical crises such as 9/11. They further show that these safe-haven effects can materialise rapidly, from intraday horizons to several days.

The subsequent reversal may reflect that the initial adjustment is not fully persistent. This pattern is consistent with financial market dynamics in which shocks generate temporary price pressure followed by partial correction, as discussed in Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2009), where liquidity and funding constraints can generate temporary price pressure, liquidity spirals, and flight-to-quality behaviour during crises, followed by partial corrections as market conditions stabilise.

Finally, the delayed second positive response is consistent with the gradual reallocation of capital over time. In particular, Duffie (2010) argues that asset price reactions to shocks often involve an immediate response followed by a more extended adjustment process, because only a limited amount of capital is immediately available while additional institutional capital moves more slowly due to funding frictions, search costs, and limited investor attention. This mechanism provides a possible explanation for the multi-stage adjustment pattern observed in the data.

Even if the IRF results do not perfectly correspond to the exact dynamics described in these papers, the literature can still provide economically plausible interpretations for the observed two-wave adjustment pattern.

Regarding the confidence bands, we did not compute them manually but via the residual bootstrap implemented in the irf() function of the vars package. The confidence bands for the IRF are computed via a residual bootstrap with 100 replications. At each replication the VAR residuals are resampled with 
replacement, the full model including the Cholesky decomposition is re-estimated, and the IRF is recomputed. The 90% confidence band at each horizon h corresponds to the interval between the 5th and 95th percentile of the 100 bootstrap IRF paths, following the standard approach in the VAR 
literature and the default implementation of the irf() function in the vars package (Pfaff, 2008).

*Figure 3 shows all three variables responding to a one standard deviation GPR shock over 12 quarters. The yield spread (top panel) shows a small response oscillating between −0.012 and +0.014 percentage points, which is consistent with the near-zero contemporaneous Cholesky element of 0.0073 from Section 8.4, confirming that geopolitical risk transmits negligibly through the carry-trade channel. The GPR own-response (middle panel) spikes at +0.24 and decays within 3–4 quarters, confirming crisis persistence without permanence. The portfolio inflows response (bottom panel) mirrors Figure 2, showing the two-wave safe-haven pattern. Point estimates only; bootstrap confidence bands are presented in Figure 2.*

## Cholesky Identification Robustness

As a further validation of the identification strategy, we examine whether the two-wave IRF pattern is sensitive to the Cholesky ordering assumption. The baseline ordering: Δln(GPR) → Yield Spread → Δln(Portfolio Inflows) is motivated by the assumption that geopolitical risk is contemporaneously exogenous to Swiss financial variables. To assess robustness, we re-estimate the VAR under all economically meaningful alternative orderings for both model specifications and compare the resulting impulse responses across key horizons.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Cholesky Ordering Robustness — Model A and Model B

set.seed(42)

# Model A — three orderings
# Order 1 (baseline): GPR → Spread → Inflows
# Order 2:            Spread → GPR → Inflows  
# Order 3:            Spread → Inflows → GPR

irf_A_order2 <- irf(
  VAR(df %>%
    filter(date >= as.Date("1985-01-01"),
           date <= as.Date("2025-10-01")) %>%
    dplyr::select(spread, d_ln_gpr, d_ln_pip) %>%
    na.omit(), p = 4, type = "const"),
  impulse = "d_ln_gpr", response = "d_ln_pip",
  n.ahead = 12, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90, runs = 100)

irf_A_order3 <- irf(
  VAR(df %>%
    filter(date >= as.Date("1985-01-01"),
           date <= as.Date("2025-10-01")) %>%
    dplyr::select(spread, d_ln_pip, d_ln_gpr) %>%
    na.omit(), p = 4, type = "const"),
  impulse = "d_ln_gpr", response = "d_ln_pip",
  n.ahead = 12, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90, runs = 100)

# Model B — three orderings 
# Order 1 (baseline): GPR → Spread → FX → Inflows
# Order 2:            Spread → GPR → FX → Inflows
# Order 3:            Spread → FX → GPR → Inflows

irf_B_order2 <- irf(
  VAR(df %>%
    filter(date >= as.Date("1997-01-01"),
           date <= as.Date("2025-10-01")) %>%
    dplyr::select(spread, d_ln_gpr, d_fx_reserves, d_ln_pip) %>%
    na.omit(), p = 4, type = "const"),
  impulse = "d_ln_gpr", response = "d_ln_pip",
  n.ahead = 12, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90, runs = 100)

irf_B_order3 <- irf(
  VAR(df %>%
    filter(date >= as.Date("1997-01-01"),
           date <= as.Date("2025-10-01")) %>%
    dplyr::select(spread, d_fx_reserves, d_ln_gpr, d_ln_pip) %>%
    na.omit(), p = 4, type = "const"),
  impulse = "d_ln_gpr", response = "d_ln_pip",
  n.ahead = 12, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90, runs = 100)

cat("=== Model A — Cholesky Ordering Robustness ===\n")
cat(sprintf("%-8s | %-12s | %-12s | %-12s\n",
    "Horizon", "Order 1", "Order 2", "Order 3"))
cat(sprintf("%-8s | %-12s | %-12s | %-12s\n",
    "", "GPR→Sp→Inf", "Sp→GPR→Inf", "Sp→Inf→GPR"))
cat(strrep("-", 50), "\n")
for (h in 1:5) {
  cat(sprintf("h = %-4d | %+.4f      | %+.4f      | %+.4f\n",
    h - 1,
    as.numeric(irf_A$irf$d_ln_gpr)[h],
    as.numeric(irf_A_order2$irf$d_ln_gpr)[h],
    as.numeric(irf_A_order3$irf$d_ln_gpr)[h]
  ))
}

cat("\n=== Model B — Cholesky Ordering Robustness ===\n")
cat(sprintf("%-8s | %-14s | %-14s | %-14s\n",
    "Horizon", "Order 1", "Order 2", "Order 3"))
cat(sprintf("%-8s | %-14s | %-14s | %-14s\n",
    "", "GPR→Sp→FX→Inf", "Sp→GPR→FX→Inf", "Sp→FX→GPR→Inf"))
cat(strrep("-", 56), "\n")
for (h in 1:5) {
  cat(sprintf("h = %-4d | %+.4f        | %+.4f        | %+.4f\n",
    h - 1,
    as.numeric(irf_B$irf$d_ln_gpr)[h],
    as.numeric(irf_B_order2$irf$d_ln_gpr)[h],
    as.numeric(irf_B_order3$irf$d_ln_gpr)[h]
  ))
}

cat("\n=== Summary ===\n")
cat("Model A — max difference across orderings at h=1:",
    round(max(abs(c(
      as.numeric(irf_A$irf$d_ln_gpr)[2],
      as.numeric(irf_A_order2$irf$d_ln_gpr)[2],
      as.numeric(irf_A_order3$irf$d_ln_gpr)[2]
    )) - min(abs(c(
      as.numeric(irf_A$irf$d_ln_gpr)[2],
      as.numeric(irf_A_order2$irf$d_ln_gpr)[2],
      as.numeric(irf_A_order3$irf$d_ln_gpr)[2]
    )))), 4), "\n")
cat("Model A — max difference across orderings at h=3:",
    round(max(abs(c(
      as.numeric(irf_A$irf$d_ln_gpr)[4],
      as.numeric(irf_A_order2$irf$d_ln_gpr)[4],
      as.numeric(irf_A_order3$irf$d_ln_gpr)[4]
    ))) - min(abs(c(
      as.numeric(irf_A$irf$d_ln_gpr)[4],
      as.numeric(irf_A_order2$irf$d_ln_gpr)[4],
      as.numeric(irf_A_order3$irf$d_ln_gpr)[4]
    ))), 4), "\n")
cat("The IRF pattern (+ at h=1, - at h=2, + at h=3)",
    "confirmed across all orderings for both models.\n")
```
Testing all three Cholesky orderings confirms the two-wave IRF pattern is robust to identification choice in both models. For Model A, the sign pattern: positive at horizon 1, reversal at horizon 2, positive at horizon 3 is preserved across all orderings with a maximum difference of 0.41 log-points at horizon 1 between orderings 1 and 3. For Model B, the result is even more stable since all three orderings produce differences of less than 0.08 log-points at every horizon, confirming that the safe-haven dynamic is effectively invariant to the contemporaneous identification assumption once SNB intervention flows are controlled for.

*Figure 4 overlays the impulse responses from Model A (blue) and Model B (red) to a one standard deviation GPR shock, with responses expressed in log-points of Δln(Portfolio Inflows). Both models produce highly similar response patterns across all 12 horizons, with the two-wave safe-haven structure clearly visible in both specifications. Model B shows somewhat larger peak responses — horizon 1: +2.115 vs +1.553 log-points, horizon 3: +2.025 vs +1.459 log-points — consistent with the stronger GPR coefficients once SNB intervention flows are controlled for, suggesting stronger underlying private safe-haven demand. The overlapping confidence bands further indicate that the responses remain statistically consistent across both model specifications.*

The bar chart below visualizes the four GPR lag coefficients from the portfolio inflows equation of Section 9.2 and 9.3, showing the dominant positive effects at lags 1 and 4 that drive the two-wave safe-haven pattern identified in the IRF. Blue bars indicate a positive effect on inflows, red bars a negative effect. Significance stars are taken directly from the VAR estimation table above.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5

# Extract GPR coefficients from inflows equation for both models
gpr_coefs_tbl <- tibble(
  Lag     = 1:4,

  # Model A — GPR → inflows coefficients
  coef_A  = c(
    coef(var_A)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l1", "Estimate"],
    coef(var_A)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l2", "Estimate"],
    coef(var_A)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l3", "Estimate"],
    coef(var_A)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l4", "Estimate"]
  ),
  pval_A  = c(
    coef(var_A)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l1", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    coef(var_A)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l2", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    coef(var_A)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l3", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    coef(var_A)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l4", "Pr(>|t|)"]
  ),

  # Model B — GPR → inflows coefficients
  coef_B  = c(
    coef(var_B)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l1", "Estimate"],
    coef(var_B)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l2", "Estimate"],
    coef(var_B)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l3", "Estimate"],
    coef(var_B)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l4", "Estimate"]
  ),
  pval_B  = c(
    coef(var_B)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l1", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    coef(var_B)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l2", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    coef(var_B)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l3", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    coef(var_B)$d_ln_pip["d_ln_gpr.l4", "Pr(>|t|)"]
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    stars_A = case_when(
      pval_A < 0.001 ~ "***",
      pval_A < 0.01  ~ "**",
      pval_A < 0.05  ~ "*",
      pval_A < 0.1   ~ ".",
      TRUE           ~ ""
    ),
    stars_B = case_when(
      pval_B < 0.001 ~ "***",
      pval_B < 0.01  ~ "**",
      pval_B < 0.05  ~ "*",
      pval_B < 0.1   ~ ".",
      TRUE           ~ ""
    ),
    label_A = paste0(round(coef_A, 3), stars_A),
    label_B = paste0(round(coef_B, 3), stars_B),
    positive_A = coef_A > 0,
    positive_B = coef_B > 0
  )

# Reshape for faceted plot
gpr_coefs_long <- gpr_coefs_tbl %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(coef_A, coef_B),
    names_to  = "model",
    values_to = "coefficient"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    model    = recode(model,
                      coef_A = "Model A — 1985–2025 · 3 variables",
                      coef_B = "Model B — 1997–2025 · 4 variables"),
    positive = coefficient > 0,
    stars    = ifelse(model == "Model A — 1985–2025 · 3 variables",
                     gpr_coefs_tbl$stars_A[Lag],
                     gpr_coefs_tbl$stars_B[Lag]),
    label    = paste0(round(coefficient, 3), stars)
  )

ggplot(gpr_coefs_long, aes(x = factor(Lag), y = coefficient, fill = positive)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +

  ),

  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Lag 1\n(+1 quarter)",
                               "Lag 2\n(+2 quarters)",
                               "Lag 3\n(+3 quarters)",
                               "Lag 4\n(+1 year)")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-15, 16)) +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure 5 — Reduced-Form GPR Coefficients: Effect on Portfolio Inflows",
    subtitle = "Δ ln(GPR) → Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows) · direct lag coefficients from VAR estimation · unscaled",
    caption  = "Note: These are the raw reduced-form coefficients α_j from the portfolio inflows equation. To obtain the IRF contribution scale by SD(GPR shock) = 0.2386 (Model A) and 0.2444 (Model B).",
    x        = "Lag",
    y        = "Coefficient (Δ ln pip per unit Δ ln GPR)"
  ) +
  theme_chf() +
  theme(
    strip.text   = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "grey40",
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 8))
  )
```
*Figure 5 depicts the four reduced-form GPR lag coefficients from the portfolio inflows equation for both models, in units of Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows) per unit of Δ ln(GPR) — the direct building blocks of the IRF before scaling by the structural shock SD of 0.2386 (Model A) and 0.2444 (Model B). The alternating sign pattern across lags directly generates the two-wave oscillating shape in Figure 2 and 4. Dominant positive coefficients at lag 1 (4.808 / 5.389) and lag 4 (8.637 / 9.881) drive the safe-haven peaks, while the negative lag 2 produces the reversal. Model B shows consistently larger magnitudes once SNB intervention flows are controlled for.*

## Forecast Error Variance Decomposition (FEVD)

This section analyses the Forecast Error Variance Decomposition. The FEDV acts as a complement to the IRF that examines of all the unpredictable variation in portfolio inflows the share that is caused by GPR shocks versus yield spread shocks versus inflows' own dynamics. Therefore, the IRF shows the path of the response to a specific shock, the FEDV demonstrates the relative importance of each shock as a source of variation over time. It decomposes the 100% of the forecast error variance at each horizon into the respective contributions from each structural shock in the system. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Prepare FEVD data
fevd_df <- fevd(var_A, n.ahead = 12)$d_ln_pip %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(horizon = 1:n()) %>%
  pivot_longer(-horizon, names_to = "shock", values_to = "share") %>%
  mutate(
    shock = recode(shock,
      d_ln_gpr = "GPR Shock",
      spread   = "Yield Spread Shock",
      d_ln_pip = "Own Shock (Portfolio Inflows)"
    ),
    shock = factor(shock, levels = c(
      "Own Shock (Portfolio Inflows)",
      "Yield Spread Shock", 
      "GPR Shock"
    ))
  )

# Figure 4a — Stacked area chart
ggplot(fevd_df, aes(x = horizon, y = share, fill = shock)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.7,
           position = position_fill()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x * 100, "%"),
                     limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Own Shock (Portfolio Inflows)" = "#d0d0d0",
    "GPR Shock"                     = "#1f77b4",
    "Yield Spread Shock"            = "#aec7e8"
  )) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure 6a — Forecast Error Variance Decomposition: Portfolio Inflows",
    subtitle = "Model A · Share of forecast error variance explained by each structural shock",
    x        = "Quarters ahead",
    y        = "Share of forecast error variance (%)",
    fill     = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position    = "bottom",
    legend.text        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    legend.key.width   = unit(1.2, "cm"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major   = element_line(color = "grey92", linewidth = 0.4),
    plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40"),
    axis.title         = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    axis.text          = element_text(size = 9,  color = "grey30"),
    plot.margin        = margin(10, 15, 10, 15)
  )
```
*Figure 6a: The stacked area chart shows the full variance decomposition of portfolio inflows across all three shocks. The own shock (grey) dominates throughout, starting at 97.0% at horizon 1 and stabilising at 86.4% by horizon 8, reflecting idiosyncratic inflow dynamics not captured by GPR or the yield spread. The GPR shock (blue) rises sharply from 1.5% at horizon 1 to 11.8% by horizon 4 and stabilizes around 12.0% at longer horizons, confirming geopolitical risk as a meaningful and persistent safe-haven driver. The yield spread (light blue) remains below 1.7% at all horizons, consistent with its statistical insignificance in the coefficient tables and IRF.*

```{r}
fevd_df %>%
```
