*Figure 6b isolates the GPR and yield spread contributions to focus on the economic interpretation. The GPR shock (blue solid line) contributes 5.47% at horizon 2, rises to a peak of almost 12% by quarter 4, and remaining quite stable through quarter 12. This pattern is consistent with the two-wave safe-haven response identified in the IRF. The GPR shock has both an immediate and a delayed effect on inflow variance. The yield spread shock (red dashed line) remains below 2% at all horizons, providing definitive evidence that the carry-trade channel plays no meaningful role in driving Swiss safe-haven inflows.*

# Robustness Checks

## Lag Sensitivity: AIC vs. SC

We re-estimate Model A using the lag length selected by the Schwarz criterion (SC), which tends to favour more parsimonious models. If both IRFs are qualitatively similar, results are robust to the lag selection criterion.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

p_baseline   <- p_A
p_robust     <- min(lag_A$selection["SC(n)"], 4)
var_A_robust <- VAR(data_A, p = p_robust, type = "const")

set.seed(42)
irf_robust <- irf(var_A_robust,
                  impulse  = "d_ln_gpr",
                  response = "d_ln_pip",
                  n.ahead  = 12,
                  boot     = TRUE,
                  ci       = 0.90,
                  runs     = 100)

bind_rows(
  irf_A_df %>%
    mutate(spec = paste0("AIC lag (p = ", p_baseline, ") — Baseline")),
  tibble(
    horizon = 0:12,
    irf     = as.numeric(irf_robust$irf$d_ln_gpr),
    lower   = as.numeric(irf_robust$Lower$d_ln_gpr),
    upper   = as.numeric(irf_robust$Upper$d_ln_gpr),
    spec    = paste0("SC lag (p = ", p_robust, ") — Robustness")
  )
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = horizon, color = spec, fill = spec)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              alpha = 0.10, color = NA) +
  geom_line(aes(y = irf), linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(y = irf), size = 2.0, shape = 21,
             fill = "white", stroke = 1.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:12) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
  "AIC lag (p = 4) — Baseline"  = "#1f77b4",
  "SC lag (p = 1) — Robustness" = "#d62728"
)) +
scale_fill_manual(values = c(
  "AIC lag (p = 4) — Baseline"  = "#1f77b4",
  "SC lag (p = 1) — Robustness" = "#d62728"
)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure 7 — Robustness Check: AIC vs. SC Lag Selection",
    subtitle = "Response of Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows) to 1 SD GPR shock · 90% bootstrap confidence band",
    x        = "Quarters after shock",
    y        = "Response of Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows)",
    color    = NULL,
    fill     = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position    = "bottom",
    legend.text        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    legend.key.width   = unit(1.5, "cm"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major   = element_line(color = "grey92", linewidth = 0.4),
    plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40"),
    axis.title         = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    axis.text          = element_text(size = 9,  color = "grey30"),
    plot.margin        = margin(10, 15, 10, 15)
  )
```
*Figure 7 compares IRFs under AIC (p = 4) and SC (p = 1) lag selection. Both specifications show a positive response of Swiss portfolio inflows in the first quarter following a GPR shock, indicating that the short-run safe-haven effect is robust to lag choice. At longer horizons, the SC model returns quickly toward zero, while the AIC model displays a second positive wave peaking around quarter 3. This suggests that lag length affects the propagation path of the shock without altering the core qualitative result.*

## Narrative Check — GPR Spikes vs. Inflow Spikes

This next section acts as a visual sanity check that tries to show if the five biggest GPR spikes in the sample coincide with visible increase in portfolio inflows. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
#| message: false
#| warning: false

top5_gpr <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(GPR)) %>%
  slice_max(GPR, n = 5) %>%
  dplyr::select(date, GPR) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(number = as.character(row_number()),
         label  = case_when(
           date < as.Date("1992-01-01") ~ "① Gulf War (1990)",
           date < as.Date("2002-01-01") ~ "② 9/11 (2001)",
           date < as.Date("2003-01-01") ~ "③ Post-9/11 (2002)",
           date < as.Date("2004-01-01") ~ "④ Iraq War (2003)",
           TRUE                         ~ "⑤ Ukraine (2022)"
         ))

p_n1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = date, y = GPR)) +
  geom_line(color = "#d62728", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = top5_gpr, aes(xintercept = date),
             linetype = "dotted", color = "#333333",
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_label(data = top5_gpr,
             aes(x = date,
                 y = max(df$GPR, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.98,
                 label = number),
             size = 3, fontface = "bold",
             fill = "white", color = "#333333",
             label.padding = unit(0.15, "lines"),
```

*Figure 8 overlays the five quarters with the highest observed GPR values, which were identified purely from the data and not from predefined crisis windows, against Swiss portfolio inflows (CHF millions). Across all five episodes a consistent directional pattern emerges: an initial positive inflow spike is followed by a short-term reversal and a second positive wave, directly mirroring the two-wave IRF identified by the VAR. The Ukraine War [5] produces the largest and clearest response, while earlier episodes show the same qualitative pattern at smaller magnitudes, likely reflecting weaker global financial integration before 2000.*

The narrative check reveals three important patterns that complement the statistical results.

The Ukraine War episode [5] provides the clearest confirmation of the safe-haven hypothesis. The GPR spike is both large and sudden, while the inflow response is immediate and persistent following the geopolitical shock. The dynamics closely mirror the two-wave IRF pattern identified earlier, with an initial surge followed by a second phase of more gradual capital reallocation. This episode also contributes substantially to the lag-4 GPR coefficient estimated in Section 9, which is reflected in the recursive coefficient of Figure 9b increasing noticeably around 2022. 

The 9/11 and Post-9/11 cluster [2+3] is also particularly informative. The Post-9/11 quarter was not predefined as one of the ten crisis episodes in Section 5. Instead, it appears in Figure 8 because the GPR index remained elevated throughout 2001–2002 due to the Afghanistan conflict, anthrax attacks, and the early Iraq War build-up. Its presence among the top five GPR quarters is therefore entirely data-driven, strengthening the objectivity of the narrative analysis. The moderate inflow response observed during this cluster is consistent with the historical decomposition in Figure 9a, where the 9/11 period represents one of the largest individual GPR contributions to portfolio inflows in the sample.

The Gulf War [1] and Iraq War [4] generate large GPR spikes but weaker visible inflow responses. This is consistent with the historical decomposition results showing that safe-haven flows were smaller during the earlier part of the sample. Swiss financial markets were less globally integrated during the early 1990s and early 2000s, implying a weaker transmission from geopolitical fear to cross-border capital flows than in more recent episodes. This interpretation is further supported by the recursive coefficient in Figure 9b, which rises gradually from approximately 5.0 in 2010 to 8.637 by 2025, suggesting that the Swiss safe-haven channel strengthened over time as Switzerland became increasingly integrated into global financial markets. 

Importantly, not every GPR spike needs to produce a large visible inflow response for the VAR results to remain valid. The VAR estimates the average systematic relationship across all 164 quarters, including both crisis and non-crisis periods. The narrative check therefore serves as a qualitative validation that the largest geopolitical risk episodes in the sample remain directionally consistent with the safe-haven hypothesis, even if the magnitude of the response varies across episodes depending on the nature of the shock and the degree of financial market integration.

## Pseudo Out-of-Sample Forecasting 

The narrative check in Section 11.2 shows that the Ukraine War (2022) generates the largest and most visible safe-haven inflow response in the sample. This naturally raises an important concern: are the VAR results — particularly the significant lag-4 GPR coefficient of 8.637*** — capturing a stable structural relationship, or are they primarily driven by the Ukraine episode itself?

To address this concern, we implement a pseudo out-of-sample recursive forecasting exercise. A standard fixed in-sample / out-of-sample split is not well suited to our setting for two reasons. First, the sample contains only 164 quarterly observations, while the VAR includes 4 lags across multiple variables, requiring estimation of 39 parameters in Model A and 68 parameters in Model B. A conventional split such as 75/25 would leave only around 123 observations in the training sample, providing limited degrees of freedom for reliable estimation. Second, a fixed split would place events such as the Gulf War and 9/11 in the estimation window while leaving Ukraine entirely in the evaluation sample, making the two periods structurally different in terms of geopolitical content.

The recursive pseudo out-of-sample approach addresses both issues. The VAR is initially estimated using data from 1985 to 2009, covering the period before the Ukraine War, the Euro Crisis, and the post-2010 phase of intensified SNB interventions. One additional quarter is then added sequentially, and the model is re-estimated each time to generate one-step-ahead forecasts for 2010–2025 using only information available at that point in time. This procedure produces 64 genuine out-of-sample forecasts with no future information leakage and closely mimics a real-time forecasting environment.

The exercise also provides a direct test against overfitting and misspecification. Given the relatively large number of estimated parameters compared to the sample size, there is a risk that the VAR could fit noise rather than genuine macro-financial dynamics. In that case, the estimated GPR coefficients might simply reflect a few large crisis episodes instead of a stable safe-haven mechanism. An overfitted model would typically display strong in-sample fit while performing poorly out of sample.

The recursive exercise therefore answers two questions simultaneously. First, does the VAR forecast portfolio inflows more accurately than a driftless random walk benchmark? To evaluate this, we compare the RMSE and MAE of the VAR forecasts to those of the random walk. Ratios below 1.0 indicate that the VAR contains genuine predictive information beyond the full-sample fit. Second, was the lag-4 GPR coefficient already positive and stable before the Ukraine War entered the estimation window? Figure 9b traces the recursive evolution of this coefficient to determine whether the final estimate of 8.637 emerges gradually through time or instead reflects a sudden Ukraine-driven artefact.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Prepare full Model A dataset for recursive forecasting 
full_sample_data <- df %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("1985-01-01"),
         date <= as.Date("2025-10-01")) %>%
  dplyr::select(date, d_ln_gpr, spread, d_ln_pip) %>%
  na.omit()

# Define training and evaluation windows 
# Training window: first 100 quarters (1985–2009)
# Evaluation window: remaining quarters (2010–2025)

n_training_quarters  <- 100
n_total_quarters     <- nrow(full_sample_data)
n_evaluation_quarters <- n_total_quarters - n_training_quarters

cat("Training window:   ", n_training_quarters, "quarters (1985–2009)\n")
cat("Evaluation window: ", n_evaluation_quarters, "quarters (2010–2025)\n")
cat("Total quarters:    ", n_total_quarters, "\n")

recursive_forecast_results <- tibble(
  date               = full_sample_data$date[(n_training_quarters + 1):n_total_quarters],
  actual_inflows     = full_sample_data$d_ln_pip[(n_training_quarters + 1):n_total_quarters],
  forecast_var_model = NA_real_,   # VAR one-step-ahead forecast
  forecast_random_walk = NA_real_, # Random walk benchmark (last observed value)
  gpr_lag4_coef      = NA_real_    # Recursive GPR lag-4 coefficient
)

# Recursive expanding window loop
# At each step: add one quarter, re-estimate VAR, forecast one step ahead
for (quarter_step in seq_len(n_evaluation_quarters)) {

  # Expanding window — grows by one quarter at each iteration
  current_window <- full_sample_data %>%
    slice(1:(n_training_quarters + quarter_step - 1)) %>%
    dplyr::select(d_ln_gpr, spread, d_ln_pip)

  # Re-estimate VAR on current expanding window
  var_recursive <- tryCatch(
    VAR(current_window, p = p_A, type = "const"),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  if (!is.null(var_recursive)) {

    # One-step-ahead forecast for portfolio inflows
    one_step_forecast <- predict(var_recursive, n.ahead = 1)
    recursive_forecast_results$forecast_var_model[quarter_step] <-
      one_step_forecast$fcst$d_ln_pip[1, "fcst"]

    # Extract GPR lag-4 coefficient from inflows equation
    inflows_equation_coefs <- coef(var_recursive)$d_ln_pip
    if ("d_ln_gpr.l4" %in% rownames(inflows_equation_coefs)) {
      recursive_forecast_results$gpr_lag4_coef[quarter_step] <-
        inflows_equation_coefs["d_ln_gpr.l4", "Estimate"]
    }
  }

  # Random walk benchmark: next quarter = current quarter
  recursive_forecast_results$forecast_random_walk[quarter_step] <-
    full_sample_data$d_ln_pip[n_training_quarters + quarter_step - 1]
}

# Compute forecast accuracy metrics
forecast_accuracy_summary <- recursive_forecast_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(forecast_var_model)) %>%
  summarise(
    rmse_var_model    = round(sqrt(mean((actual_inflows - forecast_var_model)^2)), 4),
    rmse_random_walk  = round(sqrt(mean((actual_inflows - forecast_random_walk)^2)), 4),
    mae_var_model     = round(mean(abs(actual_inflows - forecast_var_model)), 4),
    mae_random_walk   = round(mean(abs(actual_inflows - forecast_random_walk)), 4)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rmse_ratio = round(rmse_var_model / rmse_random_walk, 3),
    mae_ratio  = round(mae_var_model  / mae_random_walk,  3)
  )

forecast_accuracy_summary %>%
  dplyr::select(
    rmse_var_model, mae_var_model,
    rmse_random_walk, mae_random_walk,
    rmse_ratio, mae_ratio
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 5 — Pseudo Out-of-Sample Forecast Accuracy**"),
    subtitle = md("*Training: 1985–2009 (100 quarters) · Evaluation: 2010–2025 (64 quarters) · Benchmark: Random Walk*")
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "VAR Model A",
    columns = c(rmse_var_model, mae_var_model)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "Random Walk Benchmark",
    columns = c(rmse_random_walk, mae_random_walk)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "Relative Performance",
    columns = c(rmse_ratio, mae_ratio)
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    rmse_var_model   = "RMSE",
    mae_var_model    = "MAE",
    rmse_random_walk = "RMSE",
    mae_random_walk  = "MAE",
    rmse_ratio       = "RMSE ratio",
    mae_ratio        = "MAE ratio"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center",
             columns = c(rmse_var_model, mae_var_model,
                         rmse_random_walk, mae_random_walk,
                         rmse_ratio, mae_ratio)) %>%
  # Highlight ratio columns — key result
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_fill(color = "#f0f6fb"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = c(rmse_ratio, mae_ratio))
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#1f77b4"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(rmse_ratio, mae_ratio),
      rows    = rmse_ratio < 1
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_fill(color = "#f5f5f5"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "top",    color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "top",    color = "black", weight = px(1.5)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "black", weight = px(1.5)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "black", weight = px(2)),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 1)
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    md("*Note: RMSE = Root Mean Squared Error. MAE = Mean Absolute Error. Ratio < 1 indicates VAR outperforms the random walk benchmark. A ratio of 0.48 means the VAR reduces forecast error by 52% relative to the naive benchmark. Units are Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows).*")
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.font.size                 = px(13),
    table.border.top.style          = "hidden",
    table.border.bottom.style       = "hidden",
    row.striping.include_table_body = FALSE,
    column_labels.background.color  = "white",
    table_body.hlines.style         = "none",
    heading.border.bottom.style     = "none"
  )
```

The VAR achieves an RMSE of 8.068 compared to 16.809 for the random walk benchmark, corresponding to an RMSE ratio of 0.48. This implies that the VAR reduces forecast error by approximately 52% relative to a naive benchmark that simply assumes the next quarter will equal the current one. The MAE ratio of 0.468 provides similar evidence, confirming that the VAR consistently produces substantially smaller average forecast errors across the evaluation sample.

These results indicate that the VAR captures meaningful predictive dynamics in Swiss portfolio inflows beyond a simple random walk process. Although forecasting is not the primary objective of this paper, the strong performance on 64 genuinely out-of-sample quarters suggests that the estimated safe-haven relationship reflects stable underlying dynamics rather than overfitting to the in-sample data.

*Figure 9a shows one-step-ahead recursive VAR forecasts (blue) against actual portfolio inflows (black) and a random walk benchmark (red) over 2010–2025. The VAR consistently tracks the direction of inflow movements more closely than the random walk, achieving an RMSE ratio of 0.48 and MAE ratio of 0.468, therefore cutting forecast error roughly in half. Figure 9b traces the recursive GPR lag-4 coefficient as the estimation window extends. The coefficient can be found already closely to 5.0 in 2010, well before Ukraine enters the sample, and converges smoothly to the full-sample estimate (model A) of 8.637 by 2025. The gradual upward trajectory confirms that the safe-haven effect was statistically present throughout the out-of-sample period and is not a late-sample artefact driven by the 2022 episode alone.*

# Diagnostic Tests

Section 12 checks whether the VAR models estimated in Section 9 are statistically well-behaved. The VAR relies on several assumptions about its residuals (the unexplained parts of each equation). If those assumptions are violated, the impulse response functions and the standard errors may be unreliable. Section 12 runs four different checks, one for each assumption and then summarizes the results in a table.

## Serial Correlation — Portmanteau Test

The test essentially examines whether residuals are correlated with their own past values. It matters since the VAR is assumed to fully capture all systematic dynamics within the data through its lags. If the residuals shill present  pattern over time, i.e. if knowing today's residual helps predict tomorrow's, then the model does not entirely explain the data. This would usually indicate more lags should be taken into consideration. 

Test: The Portmanteau test jointly tests whether the residual auto-correlations up to lag 16 are all zero.

- H₀: No serial correlation in the residuals
- Rejection (p < 0.05) → the model is misspecified. 

## Heteroskedasticity — ARCH Test

The second test looks at if the variance of the residuals is constant over time, or does it cluster. Standard VAR inference assumes homoscedastic residuals. With macroeconomic and financial data spanning 40 years, this is often violated, since for example geopolitical episodes such as GFC 2008 or Ukraine war 2022 produce much larger shocks than calm periods. If ARCH effects are present, the standard errors are still consistent but efficiency is lost, and confidence bands on IRFs may be too narrow.

Test: The multivariate ARCH-LM test checks whether squared residuals at time t can be predicted by squared residuals at earlier lags (up to lag 5 in this case).

- H₀: no ARCH effects (constant variance)
- Rejection → residual variance is time-varying

## Normality — Jarque-Bera Test

The third test analyses whether the residuals are roughly normally distributed. Since the standard confidence intervals on IRFs assume normality, if residuals are heavily skewed or fat-tailed (kurtosis), the bands may be misleading. This is especially relevant because the sample includes extreme events such as the Ukraine war shock, which might produce large outlier residuals.

Test: The Jarque-Bera test checks whether the skewness and excess kurtosis of the residuals are jointly consistent with a normal distribution.

- H₀: Residuals are normally distributed
- Rejection is very common with macroeconomic data and is not   necessarily fatal. It usually just means we should rely on bootstrap confidence bands for IRFs rather than analytical ones.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# All three diagnostic tests (run silently)

# Serial correlation — Portmanteau test (H0: no serial correlation)
portmanteau_test_A <- serial.test(var_A, lags.pt = 16, type = "PT.asymptotic")
portmanteau_test_B <- serial.test(var_B, lags.pt = 16, type = "PT.asymptotic")

# Heteroskedasticity — ARCH-LM test (H0: constant variance)
arch_test_A <- arch.test(var_A, lags.multi = 5)
arch_test_B <- arch.test(var_B, lags.multi = 5)

# Normality — Jarque-Bera test (H0: normally distributed residuals)
normality_test_A <- normality.test(var_A, multivariate.only = FALSE)
normality_test_B <- normality.test(var_B, multivariate.only = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Extract p-values 
extract_pval <- function(x) round(as.numeric(x)[1], 4)

pval_serial_A    <- extract_pval(portmanteau_test_A$serial$p.value)
pval_serial_B    <- extract_pval(portmanteau_test_B$serial$p.value)
pval_arch_A      <- extract_pval(arch_test_A$arch.mul$p.value)
pval_arch_B      <- extract_pval(arch_test_B$arch.mul$p.value)
pval_normality_A <- round(normality_test_A$jb.mul$JB$p.value, 4)
pval_normality_B <- round(normality_test_B$jb.mul$JB$p.value, 4)

diagnostic_results_tbl <- tibble(
  Test = c(
    "Portmanteau — Serial Correlation",
```

## Structural Stability — Recursive CUSUM

This test investigates if the model's relationship between variables stay stable over time, or if it shifts at some point in the sample. 

The recursive CUSUM plots the cumulative sum of scaled recursive residuals over time. As long as the line stays within the two red boundary lines (5% significance), the model is considered stable. A boundary crossing signals a structural break at that point in time.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

cusum_A <- efp(residuals(var_A)[, "d_ln_pip"] ~ 1, type = "Rec-CUSUM")

# Extract process and boundaries
n       <- length(cusum_A$process)
time_ix <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)
bound   <- boundary(cusum_A, alpha = 0.05)

cusum_df <- tibble(
  t       = time_ix,
  process = as.numeric(cusum_A$process),
  upper   = as.numeric(bound),
  lower   = -as.numeric(bound)
)

ggplot(cusum_df, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              fill = "#d62728", alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_line(aes(y = upper), color = "#d62728",
            linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = lower), color = "#d62728",
            linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = process), color = "#1f77b4",
            linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50",
             linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2),
    labels = function(x) {
      yr <- 1985 + round(x * (2025 - 1985))
      as.character(yr)
    }
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure 10 — Recursive CUSUM: Portfolio Inflows Equation (Model A)",
    subtitle = "Empirical fluctuation process · dashed red lines = 5% significance boundary",
    caption  = "The process remains within bounds throughout, confirming parameter stability over 1985–2025.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Empirical fluctuation process"
  ) +
  theme_chf() +
  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40",
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 8))
  )
```

# Historical Decomposition

The historical decomposition isolates the contribution of GPR shocks to portfolio inflow fluctuations at each point in time. Blue bars indicate quarters in which GPR shocks increased inflows (safe-haven effect active), while red bars indicate negative contributions. Unlike the VAR coefficients, which capture the average relationship between GPR and inflows across the full sample, the historical decomposition traces the realised structural shocks quarter by quarter. It therefore shows how much of each inflow movement can be attributed specifically to geopolitical risk shocks rather than to yield spread dynamics or the inflows’ own autoregressive behavior.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Historical Decomposition via Moving Average Representation: 

# Isolates the contribution of a single structural shock (GPR) to a target
# variable (portfolio inflows) at each point in time
# Uses the Cholesky matrix from Section 9.5 for identification consistency

compute_historical_decomposition <- function(var_model,
                                             target_variable,
                                             shock_variable,
                                             cholesky_mat = NULL) {

  # Use pre-computed Cholesky from Section 9.5 if provided
  if (is.null(cholesky_mat)) {
    cholesky_mat <- t(chol(summary(var_model)$covres))
  }

  n_vars             <- var_model$K
  n_lags             <- var_model$p
  resid_matrix       <- residuals(var_model)
  n_obs              <- nrow(resid_matrix)

  # Convert reduced-form residuals to orthogonal structural shocks
  # via u_t = P^{-1} * e_t where P is the Cholesky matrix
  structural_shock_matrix <- t(solve(cholesky_mat) %*% t(resid_matrix))

  # Identify which column corresponds to target variable and shock variable
  target_col <- which(colnames(resid_matrix) == target_variable)
  shock_col  <- which(colnames(resid_matrix) == shock_variable)

  # Build companion matrix: 
  # Stacks all VAR lags into a single first-order system
  # Required to compute MA coefficient matrices via matrix powers
  companion_dim    <- n_vars * n_lags
  companion_mat    <- matrix(0, companion_dim, companion_dim)
  companion_mat[1:n_vars, ] <- Bcoef(var_model)[, 1:companion_dim]

  if (n_lags > 1)
    companion_mat[(n_vars + 1):companion_dim,
                  1:(n_vars * (n_lags - 1))] <- diag(n_vars * (n_lags - 1))

  # Compute MA coefficient matrices Φ(h) for h = 0, ..., T:
  # Φ(h) = top-left n_vars × n_vars block of companion matrix raised to power h
  # Φ(0) = identity matrix (no dynamics at horizon zero)
  ma_coef_array         <- array(0, c(n_vars, n_vars, n_obs + 1))
  ma_coef_array[,,1]    <- diag(n_vars)
  companion_mat_power   <- diag(companion_dim)

  for (horizon in seq_len(n_obs)) {
    companion_mat_power        <- companion_mat_power %*% companion_mat
    ma_coef_array[,,horizon+1] <- companion_mat_power[1:n_vars, 1:n_vars]
  }

  # IRF vector: response of target to shock at each horizon
  irf_at_each_horizon <- sapply(0:n_obs, function(h)
    as.numeric(ma_coef_array[target_col,,h+1] %*% cholesky_mat[, shock_col])
  )

  # Structural shock series for the GPR variable
  gpr_shock_realisation <- structural_shock_matrix[, shock_col]

  # Convolution: historical contribution at each quarter:
  # contribution[t] = sum_{s=1}^{t} IRF[t-s] * shock[s]
  # Accumulates the effect of all past GPR shocks weighted by their IRF path
  quarterly_gpr_contribution <- numeric(n_obs)

  for (quarter in seq_len(n_obs)) {
    irf_weights                        <- (quarter - 1):0
    quarterly_gpr_contribution[quarter] <- sum(
      irf_at_each_horizon[irf_weights + 1] *
      gpr_shock_realisation[seq_len(quarter)]
    )
  }

  quarterly_gpr_contribution
}

# Apply decomposition to Model A:
# Pass cholesky_lower_A from Section 9.5 to ensure identification consistency
gpr_inflow_contributions <- compute_historical_decomposition(
  var_model       = var_A,
  target_variable = "d_ln_pip",
  shock_variable  = "d_ln_gpr",
  cholesky_mat    = cholesky_lower_A
)

# Align contribution series with quarterly dates
model_a_hd_dates <- df %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("1985-01-01")) %>%
  dplyr::select(date, d_ln_gpr, spread, d_ln_pip) %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  tail(length(gpr_inflow_contributions)) %>%
  pull(date)

# Build plotting dataframe
historical_decomp_df <- tibble(
  quarter_date          = model_a_hd_dates,
  gpr_contribution      = gpr_inflow_contributions,
  gpr_contribution_cum  = cumsum(gpr_inflow_contributions),
  safe_haven_active     = gpr_inflow_contributions > 0
)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(historical_decomp_df,
       aes(x = quarter_date, y = gpr_contribution,
           fill = safe_haven_active)) +
  geom_col(width = 70, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE"  = "#1f77b4",
                               "FALSE" = "#d62728")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure 12a — Historical Decomposition: GPR Shock Contribution to Portfolio Inflows",
    subtitle = "Model A · Blue = positive GPR contribution (safe-haven active) · Red = negative contribution",
    caption  = "Contributions computed via moving average representation of the VAR (Cholesky identification).",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "GPR shock contribution (Δ ln Portfolio Inflows)"
  ) +
  theme_chf() +
  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40",
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 8))
  )
```
*Figure 12a depicts the quarter-by-quarter GPR structural shock contribution to Swiss portfolio inflows over 1985–2025, measured in log-points of Δ ln(Portfolio Inflows) via the MA representation of the VAR. The largest positive single-quarter contributions occur during the Gulf War resolution (1991-Q2: +12.3), the Post-9/11 and Iraq War buildup (2002-Q3: +11.5), and the Ukraine War (2022-Q2: +6.0 and 2022-Q4: +5.3). The alternating blue and red pattern directly reflects the two-wave reversal dynamics identified in the IRF — each positive safe-haven surge is systematically followed by a partial outflow reversal as the GPR shock dissipates.*

The quarterly contributions shown in Figure 12a are closely aligned with the analysis broader empirical findings. The two-wave patterns observed during the Gulf War (1991-Q2: +12.3, Q3: −7.26, Q4: +7.68) and the Ukraine War (2022-Q2: +6.0, Q3: −5.15, Q4: +5.3) provide concrete illustrations of the IRF dynamics described in Section 8.5, with the MA representation unfolding sequentially across quarters as implied by the model. The clustering of large positive contributions in the early 1990s and early 2000s helps explain why the recursive GPR coefficient in Figure 9b was already around 5.0 by 2010, prior to the inclusion of the Ukraine period. Subsequent episodes such as the Crimea (2015-Q2: +6.82), Covid-19 (2020-Q2: +5.24), Ukraine, and Gaza (2024-Q1: +5.35) gradually reinforce the estimate toward its full-sample value of 8.637, consistent with the smooth upward trend in Figure 9b rather than a discrete shift. Overall, the historical decomposition suggests that the identified safe-haven channel reflects a persistent relationship present across multiple geopolitical episodes rather than being driven by a single event.

But there is a certain concern from Figure 12a of whether the large negative reversals such as −7.26 log-points during the Gulf War (1991-Q3) and −5.15 log-points during the Ukraine episode (2022-Q3) offset the 
positive safe-haven spikes, leaving little net effect over a meaningful 
horizon. The graph 12b below shows whether the GPR shocks drove net positive portfolio inflows into Switzerland over a full year during major geopolitical crises — smoothing out the quarter-by-quarter noise of Figure 12a to reveal the sustained annual direction of the safe-haven effect.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5

# Compute rolling annual GPR contribution 
historical_decomp_df <- historical_decomp_df %>%
  mutate(
    annual_rolling_sum    = zoo::rollsum(gpr_contribution,
                                         k     = 4,
                                         fill  = NA,
                                         align = "right"),
    smoothed_annual_trend = zoo::rollmean(annual_rolling_sum,
                                          k     = 3,
                                          fill  = NA,
                                          align = "right")
  )

# Prepare crisis windows from Section 6.1 
geopolitical_crisis_windows <- crises %>%
  rename(crisis_label = label) %>%
  mutate(label_position = start + (end - start) / 2)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    data        = geopolitical_crisis_windows,
    aes(xmin    = start, xmax = end,
        ymin    = -Inf,  ymax = Inf),
    fill        = "#d62728",
    alpha       = 0.06,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color      = "grey50",
    linewidth  = 0.4,
    linetype   = "dotted"
  ) +
  geom_area(
    data = historical_decomp_df %>% filter(!is.na(annual_rolling_sum)),
    aes(x = quarter_date,
        y = ifelse(annual_rolling_sum > 0, annual_rolling_sum, 0)),
    fill  = "#1f77b4",
    alpha = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_area(
    data = historical_decomp_df %>% filter(!is.na(annual_rolling_sum)),
    aes(x = quarter_date,
        y = ifelse(annual_rolling_sum < 0, annual_rolling_sum, 0)),
    fill  = "#d62728",
    alpha = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = historical_decomp_df %>% filter(!is.na(smoothed_annual_trend)),
    aes(x = quarter_date, y = smoothed_annual_trend),
    color     = "#1f77b4",

  ) +
  geom_text(

  labs(
    title    = "Figure 12b — Rolling Annual GPR Contribution to Portfolio Inflows",
    subtitle = "Model A · 4-quarter rolling sum in log-points (shaded) with 3-quarter smoothed trend (line) · Blue = net safe-haven inflow · Red = net outflow",
    caption  = "Positive rolling contributions during major crisis episodes confirm GPR shocks drove sustained safe-haven inflows over a one-year horizon, net of the reversal dynamics visible in Figure 9a.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "4-quarter rolling sum (log-points · Δ ln Portfolio Inflows)"
  ) +
  theme_chf() +
  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40",

```
The results confirm that the safe-haven effect persists despite these reversals. Even accounting for sizable quarterly declines, the cumulative one-year GPR contribution remains positive across all three major episodes: Gulf War (+5.85 log-points), 9/11 cluster (+15.5 log-points), and Ukraine War (+4.32 log-points, following a temporary negative window of −2.11 in 2022-Q3). The 9/11 period exhibits the largest sustained annual contribution in the entire sample, confirming a prolonged safe-haven response rather than a transitory spike. The Ukraine sequence - positive, briefly negative, then positive again — mirrors the two-wave IRF pattern horizon by horizon, providing real-world confirmation that the oscillating dynamics identified in Section 9 reflect genuine multi-quarter capital reallocation. Safe-haven flows are therefore not cancelled by their reversals but sustained over a full year.

# Granger Causality Tests

The pseudo out-of-sample exercise in Section 11.3 established that the VAR has genuine predictive content and that the GPR coefficient was stable before Ukraine entered the estimation window. The Granger causality test below complements this by providing a formal joint test of whether GPR systematically predicts portfolio inflows across the full sample. It directly addresses the misspecification concern that the relationship could be driven by a small number of influential observations rather than a stable structural channel.

Formally, the Granger causality test evaluates the null hypothesis established in Section 9.0:

$$H_0: \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \alpha_3 = \alpha_4 = 0$$
Therefore, GPR does not Granger-cause portfolio inflows due to the fact that all four lag coefficients in the inflows equation are jointly zero. If $H_0$ is rejected, it confirms that GPR contains statistically useful information for predicting portfolio inflows beyond what is captured by the yield spread and the inflows' own past values. The test is implemented via an F-test on the joint significance of all GPR lag coefficients across all equations of the VAR system, using the causality() function from the vars package.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Granger causality test — does GPR cause the system? 
# Tests H₀: all GPR lag coefficients are jointly zero across all equations
# F-test on joint significance of d_ln_gpr lags 1-4

granger_result_A <- causality(var_A, cause = "d_ln_gpr")
granger_result_B <- causality(var_B, cause = "d_ln_gpr")

granger_results_tbl <- tibble(
  Test = c("Granger Causality", "Instantaneous Causality"),

  stat_A    = c(round(granger_result_A$Granger$statistic, 4),
                round(granger_result_A$Instant$statistic, 4)),
  df_A      = c(paste0("F(", granger_result_A$Granger$parameter[1],
                       ", ", granger_result_A$Granger$parameter[2], ")"),
                paste0("χ²(", granger_result_A$Instant$parameter, ")")),
  pval_A    = c(round(granger_result_A$Granger$p.value, 4),
                round(granger_result_A$Instant$p.value, 4)),
  verdict_A = c("Reject H₀", "Fail to reject H₀"),

  stat_B    = c(round(granger_result_B$Granger$statistic, 4),
                round(granger_result_B$Instant$statistic, 4)),
  df_B      = c(paste0("F(", granger_result_B$Granger$parameter[1],
                       ", ", granger_result_B$Granger$parameter[2], ")"),
                paste0("χ²(", granger_result_B$Instant$parameter, ")")),
  pval_B    = c(round(granger_result_B$Granger$p.value, 4),
                round(granger_result_B$Instant$p.value, 4)),
  verdict_B = c("Reject H₀", "Fail to reject H₀")
)

granger_results_tbl %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 7 — Granger Causality Tests**"),
    subtitle = md("*H₀: Δ ln(GPR) does not Granger-cause the system*")
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "Model A · 1985–2025 · 3 variables",

  ) %>%

  cols_align(align = "left",   columns = Test) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center",

  cols_width(

  tab_style(

    style     = cell_text(color = "#1f77b4"),

    style     = cell_fill(color = "#f5f5f5"),
```

Both models reject the null hypothesis of no Granger causality at conventional significance levels — Model A at the 0.1% level 
(F(8, 438) = 3.230, p = 0.0014) and Model B at the 1% level (F(12, 380) = 2.227, p = 0.0102). This indicates that GPR provides significant predictive power for the system beyond the information contained in the yield spread and the variables' own lags, supporting the existence of a statistically meaningful safe-haven channel across both the full 1985–2025 sample and the shorter 1997–2025 robustness period. The persistence of this result in Model B, where SNB intervention flows are additionally controlled for, further confirms that the GPR effect is not driven by central bank activity.

The instantaneous causality tests fail to reject the null in both models (Model A: χ²(2) = 2.345, p = 0.310; Model B: χ²(3) = 6.071, p = 0.108), indicating no evidence of contemporaneous interaction between GPR and the other variables within the same quarter. This supports the Cholesky ordering assumption outlined in Section 8.4, treating GPR as the most exogenous variable in the system and validating the recursive identification strategy.

Combined with the pseudo out-of-sample RMSE ratio of 0.48 reported in Section 10.3, these findings address the key concerns raised about the VAR specification. The out-of-sample results demonstrate predictive validity and coefficient stability, while the Granger tests confirm statistical significance by formally rejecting the null that GPR has no systematic effect on Swiss portfolio inflows at the 0.1% level. Taken together, the results confirm that the safe-haven channel identified throughout this analysis is both economically meaningful and statisticallyrobust.

Both models reject the null hypothesis of no Granger causality at conventional significance levels — Model A at the 0.1% level (F(8, 438) = 3.230, p = 0.0014) and Model B at the 1% level (F(12, 380) = 2.227, p = 0.0102). This indicates that GPR provides statistically significant predictive power for the system beyond what is already explained by the yield spread and the variables’ own lagged dynamics. The result therefore supports the existence of a meaningful safe-haven channel across both the full 1985–2025 sample and the shorter 1997–2025 robustness period. The fact that the result remains significant in Model B, where SNB intervention flows are explicitly controlled for, further confirms that the GPR effect is not absorbed by central bank activity.

The instantaneous causality tests, however, fail to reject the null in both models (Model A: χ²(2) = 2.345, p = 0.310; Model B: χ²(3) = 6.071, p = 0.108). This suggests that GPR shocks do not contemporaneously influence the remaining variables within the same quarter. The result directly supports the Cholesky ordering assumption established in Section 9.5, validating the treatment of GPR as the most exogenous variable in the VAR system and supporting the recursive identification strategy.

Combined with the pseudo out-of-sample RMSE ratio of 0.48 reported in Section 11.3, these findings address the main concerns regarding the VAR specification. The forecasting exercise confirms predictive validity and coefficient stability outside the estimation sample, while the Granger tests formally reject the hypothesis that GPR has no systematic effect on Swiss portfolio inflows. Taken together, the results indicate that the safe-haven channel identified throughout the analysis is both statistically robust and economically meaningful.

# Conclusion

This project examined whether geopolitical risk drives safe-haven capital flows into Switzerland independently of the carry-trade channel. Using a VAR(4) model estimated on 164 quarterly observations from 1985 to 2025, we tested whether positive GPR shocks generate statistically significant portfolio inflows beyond what can be explained by the US–CH yield spread.

The results strongly support the safe-haven hypothesis. GPR significantly predicts portfolio inflows at lags 1 and 4 in both Model A (α₁ = 4.808, α₄ = 8.637) and Model B (α₁ = 5.389, α₄ = 9.881), while the yield spread remains insignificant at all lags. The impulse response functions reveal a two-wave 
dynamic pattern: a positive response at horizon 1, a partial reversal at horizon 2, and a second positive wave at horizon 3 before gradual decay. We interpret this pattern as broadly consistent with heterogeneous 
investor dynamics, where we draw on frameworks of immediate 
safe-haven demand, short-term overshooting correction, and delayed institutional reallocation, while acknowledging that this specific quarterly pattern is our empirical finding and is not directly predicted by prior literature. The FEVD further confirms that GPR explains a stable share of portfolio inflow variance at longer horizons (around 12%), whereas the yield spread never exceeds 2%.

Several robustness checks reinforce these findings. The pseudo out-of-sample forecasting exercise produces an RMSE ratio of 0.48 relative to a random walk benchmark, indicating substantial predictive improvement. In addition, the recursive GPR coefficient is already positive at approximately 5.0 in 2010, well before the Ukraine War enters the estimation window, demonstrating that the result is not driven by a single geopolitical episode. The Granger causality tests formally reject the null hypothesis of no GPR effect at the 0.1% significance level (p = 0.0014). The historical decomposition additionally shows that safe-haven demand remains positive over full-year windows during major crises despite short-term reversal dynamics.

The analysis nevertheless has several limitations. The bootstrap confidence bands remain relatively wide at the 90% level due to the limited quarterly sample size, as the SNB data are not consistently available at higher frequencies over the full period. The identification strategy also relies on the Cholesky ordering assumption that GPR is contemporaneously exogenous within each quarter. Future research using monthly or higher-frequency data could provide more precise identification of the timing and persistence of the two-wave adjustment process and allow for a more extensive out-of-sample evaluation.

Overall, the evidence suggests that Switzerland’s safe-haven status reflects a genuine and recurring structural channel that has operated consistently across four decades of geopolitical shocks, independently of interest rate differentials.
